en: Now, within the section on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the *Śrītattvaprabhāvalī*, [the author discusses] verbal testimony (*śabda*):

"Verbal testimony, whether endowed with its own primary meaning through direct denotation (*śakti*) or through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), brings about the cognition of the expressed object and is the instrument for all worldly transaction. (472)
Pervasive and situated in space, its qualities are non-different from space;
aided by lightning and wind, it becomes manifest, though otherwise it exists subtly in the ether.
Bound by its causes in water, earth, fire, and air,
sound is perceivable by the ear, consists of syllables and so forth, and is preceded by that which is unperceivable.
The streams of sound, moving upward, are perceived on mountains and other places with distinct transitions of increasing and decreasing intensity. (475)
Therefore, sounds arise from the ten directions, equal on all sides—whether soft, sweet, or harsh—and according to their respective order and species. (476)
But who indeed is that which, following after causes everywhere and being distinct,
is considered to be all-pervasive, attaining infinity, and existing in innumerable forms?
They are both worldly and conditioned, yet have been arranged by the learned.
These lines, understood by people, have been established for a suitable object that is capable of being used in linguistic convention. (478)

The nature of sound (*śabdatva*) consists in possessing a genus that is delimited by being perceivable solely by the auditory faculty; the nature of sound consists in being a quality of space (*ākāśa*); the nature of sound consists in being the object of the cognition produced by the word "sound"; and the nature of sound consists in being a quality perceived through the intuition "I hear. The fifty-two letters beginning with *ka* are accepted by the authorities (*prāmāṇika*). Each of these, when combined with the vowels, forms twelve syllables (*akṣarī*). When conjoined [with consonants], they take the form of words such as "sound" (*śabda*). Aggregates of words take the form of sentences (*vākya*). Aggregates of sentences take the form of verses (*śloka*), prose (*gadya*), treatises (*prakaraṇa*), and so forth, as well as the form of entire scriptures (*śāstra*). All of these exist, each endowed with its own respective meaning.

The word is the denoter (*vācaka*), the object is the denoted (*vācya*), and the cognition of the word is the instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). The recollection of the word-meaning produced by the word is the intermediate operation (*dvāra*). The cognition of either the function of direct denotation (*śakti*) or indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is the auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*). Verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) is the result, which is valid knowledge (*pramā*). The cognition of the word brings the word-meaning to mind by way of the cognition of one related member [of a relation]. Conventional usage (*saṃketa*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*) are the functions of the word with respect to its meaning.

And that [relation] consists in the will of God (Īśvara) in the form: "From this word, this meaning is to be understood," or "May this word cause this meaning to be understood," or "May the cognition of this meaning arise from this word."

Power (*śakti*) is the desire: "Let the object be the locus of the objective state (*viṣayatā*) produced by the cognition generated by this word. The resulting cognition is: "The object is the substratum of the particularity (*viśeṣyatā*), which is determined by the objective state residing in the object, which is determined by the objective state residing in the cognition, which is determined by the objective state residing in being-produced, which is determined by the objective state residing in the word. The relation between the word and its object is: the possession of the particularity residing in the objective state of being the object of the cognition produced by itself, as found in the objective state belonging to the will of God (*īśvarecchā*).

Now, in the second [moment], there is the desire: "Let this word be that which possesses the capacity to generate a cognition having this meaning as its object. The resulting cognition is: "The word is the substratum of the qualificand-ness (viśeṣyatā) which is determined by a capacity-ness (janakatva-niṣṭha-prakāratā), which is determined by a cognition-ness (bodha-niṣṭha-prakāratā), which is determined by a subject-ness (viṣayitva-niṣṭha-prakāratā), which is determined by a qualifier-ness (prakāratā) residing in this meaning."

In expressions such as "the word denotes the cow" (*padaṃ gāṃ vakti*) or "the cow is expressed by the word" (*padena gaur ucyate*), the denoted meaning (*vācyārtha*) is the state of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*) in God’s will—this will being determined by a mode (*prakāratā*) that consists in being the object of cognition, based on the convention: "from this word, this meaning is to be understood. In the case of "he speaks the word 'cow'" (*gāṃ padaṃ vakti*), the verbal suffix expressing the agent (*kartṛ-ākhyāta*) conveys agency (*kartṛtva*), which consists in being the locus of a mode that determines the qualificandhood through a mediated relation (*paramparayā*). This [agency] relates to the word (*pada*) in its own form (*svarūpeṇa*). The meaning of the accusative case in *gām* is "locatedness" (*niṣṭhatva*); and that locatedness which resides in the cow...

The understanding [derived from the sentence] is as follows: "The word 'cow' (gopada) is that which possesses the state of being a substratum of a modehood delimited by a qualificandumhood residing in a modehood residing in a relation of being-produced-by, which is delimited by a qualificandumhood residing in a modehood residing in a modehood delimited by a qualificandumhood residing in a modehood residing in a relation of being-defined-by, which is delimited by a modehood residing in a relation of being-defined-by, which is delimited by a qualificandumhood residing in a modehood residing in the will of God (īśvarecchīya), which is defined by a modehood residing in the state of being an object of awakening (bodhaviṣayatva-prakāratā). In this context, the meaning of the agentive suffix (kartṛ-ākhyāta) is the aforementioned substratum (āśraya).

In the statement "The word *go* denotes a cow," the aforementioned qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) is construed with the meaning [of the word] through the relation of substratum-hood (*āśrayatva*). The meaning of the instrumental case is locus-hood (*ādheyatā*). The resulting cognition is: "A cow is that which is the substratum of the qualificand-ness residing in the will of the Lord (Ishvara), as determined by the mode-hood (*prakāratā*) residing in being the object of the cognition produced by the word *go*."

Now, in cases such as "the word expresses the cow" (*padaṃ gāṃ vakti*) or "the cow is expressed by the word" (*padena gaur ucyate*), the meaning of the verbal root is the state of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*) in God's will—where that will is characterized by a mode (*prakāratā*) consisting in the capacity to produce a cognition, with the intention "may this word cause the cognition of this meaning. In the sentence "the word expresses the cow," the word "word" (*pada*) is construed as the locus of such a qualificand-ness. The resulting cognition is: "The word 'cow' is the locus of the qualificand-ness in God's will, which is characterized by a mode consisting in the capacity to produce a cognition whose object is the cow."

In the statement "The word 'go' denotes a cow," the meaning of the third case (instrumental) is *ādheyatā* (the state of being located). Therein, the word "go" is construed as the relatum (*nirūpitatva*) of that [ādheyatā]. This *ādheyatā* is construed as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). [Thus, the resulting complex is: the qualificandhood belonging to the Lord’s will (*īśvarecchīya-viśeṣyatā*), which is itself qualified by a modehood (*prakāratā*) residing in the capacity to generate cognition, and which is in turn qualified by the *ādheyatā* related to the word "go."

The cognition is as follows: "The cow" is the substratum of a qualifierhood delimited by a qualifierhood residing in a qualificandhood delimited by a qualifierhood residing in a relation of being The definition of a *pravṛttinimitta* (the ground for application) is: being denotable, while being resident in that which is denoted, and being a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the presentation of that which is denoted. In the case of the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*), the locus of the objective determination (*viśeṣyatā*) belonging to God’s will—which is determined by a qualifierhood residing in the state of being an object of cognition produced by the word "pot" as delimited by the relation of substratum (*āśrayatva*)—is the individual pot (*ghaṭa*). In the case of "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), the locus of the objective determination belonging to God’s will—which is determined by a qualifierhood residing in the state of being an object of cognition produced by the word "pot" as delimited by the relation of delimitation (*avacchedakatva*)—is pot-ness.

The objective-ness (viśeṣyatā) belonging to God’s will—which is qualified by the mode (prakāratā) residing in the state of being the object of the cognition produced by the word "pot," as delimited by the relation of being the delimitor of the delimitor of [the objective-ness]—subsists in inherence (samavāya). The forms [of this will] are: "Let the pot be the object of the cognition produced by the word 'pot'," "Let pot-ness be the delimitor of the object-ness of the cognition produced by the word 'pot'," and "Let inherence be the delimitor of the delimitor of the object-ness of the cognition produced by the word 'pot'."

In this context, it is also easy to say that the power (*śakti*) [of a word] is merely the speaker’s intention regarding the meaning of a modern convention. In the case of "The cow is the bearer of the word 'cow'," the state of being the bearer of the word 'cow' resides in the cognition of the first convention; the relation of the word 'cow' to the cow is the objectness (*viśeṣyatā*) pertaining to the convention, which is itself determined by a qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) delimited by the relation of substratumhood (*āśrayatva*) residing in the state of being the object of the understanding produced by that [convention].

By way of the relation [of the qualifier], the property of being delimited by the relation of inherence—which is itself delimited by the relation of the locus (āśrayatva) and is further delimited by the relation of the delimiting factor (avacchedakatā) as determined by the subjecthood (viśeṣyatā) residing in "cowness" (gotva)—is introduced as a qualifier.

In the second convention, the state of being the word "go" (cow) [is related] by means of a relation consisting of the property of being a convention, which is delimited by a subjecthood residing in the cognition, which is delimited by a subjecthood residing in the generative capacity, which is delimited by a subjecthood residing in the cognition, which is delimited by a subjecthood residing in the word itself, and which is delimited by a propertyhood residing in the cognition.

In this relation, as a qualifying factor, there is included the property of being delimited by the qualificandumness that is determined by the subjectness residing in "cowness" (gotva), which is itself delimited by the relation of inherence (samavāya) and has as its delimitation the subjectness residing in itself (svaniṣṭha) and delimited by the relation of objectness (viṣayatva). This [qualificandumness] resides in the cognition and is determined by the subjectness residing in the cow (go-niṣṭha-prakāratā), which is in turn delimited by the relation of objectness and has as its delimitation the subjectness residing in itself and delimited by the relation of inherence.

In the convention "let the cognition of this meaning arise from this word," the state of being a cow-word (*gopada*) [is related] by way of a relation consisting of a subjecthood (*prakāratā*) delimited by a subjecthood residing in "being produced" (*janyatva*), which is itself delimited by a subjecthood residing in the meaning, and which is further delimited by a subjecthood residing in the cognition, which is delimited by a subjecthood residing in "being produced," which is delimited by a subjecthood residing in "being produced" as qualified by its own locus through a relation of being defined (*nirūpitatva*), and which is finally delimited by a subjecthood residing in the cognition, which is delimited by the nature of cognition (*bodhatva*), and which is connected by a relation of subjecthood (*viṣayatva*).

In this context, within the qualificandumness delimited by the nature of cognition—which is itself determined by a qualifierhood residing in the cow, which is delimited by the relation of being an object (*viṣayatva*)—there is the property of being delimited by a qualificandumness that is determined by a qualifierhood residing in "cowness" (*gotva*), which is delimited by the relation of being an object whose delimitation resides in itself through the relation of inherence-inherence (*samavāya-samavāya*). This is included as a qualifier because the knowledge of denotability (*vācyatva*) is necessary for verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*).

The knowledge of denotative capacity (vācakatva) is not a requisite for verbal cognition (śābdabodha), because since inherence (samavāya) cannot be a qualifier by its own nature, the property of inherence (samavāyatva) is not presented [to consciousness]; consequently, a cognition having "cowness" (gotva) as its qualifier through the relation of inherence does not arise.

Regarding the statement "this meaning is to be understood from this word," in the view that [meaning] is denotable (*vācyatva*), the denotability consists in possessing a modehood (*prakāratā*) delimited by the relation of substratum-ness (*āśrayatva*) residing in the objectness of the cognition produced by the word, as it exists within the convention (*saṃketa*). Alternatively, denotability is the possession of a modehood delimited by the relation of substratum-ness residing in the objectness of the cognition produced by the word, as it exists within the convention.

And the state of possessing a modehood (prakāratāvattva) [is defined] by any one of the following relations: the relation delimited by the modehood that is qualified by the qualificandumness (viśeṣyatva) which is its own determiner (nirūpaka), or the relation delimited by the delimitorhood (avacchedakatva) which is delimited by itself, or the relation delimited by the relativity (saṃsargatāvacchedakatva) which is qualified by the modehood that is delimited by itself.

In the convention (saṅketa) expressed as "the cow is to be understood from the word 'cow'"—which has the sense "let the cow be the object of the cognition produced by the word 'cow'"—the property of being the object of the cognition produced by the word 'cow' is a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the cow by way of the relation of substratumhood (*āśrayatā-sambandha*); and in the cowness (*gotva*), it is a qualifier by way of the relation of delimitation (*avacchedakatā-sambandha*), which is the delimitation delimited by the delimitation residing in inherence (*samavāya*) and determined by the delimitation residing in inherence. This is according to the aforementioned convention.

The property of being a qualificand (viśeṣyatā) related to the qualifierhood (prakāratā)—which resides in the state of being the object of a cognition produced by the word "cow" (go-śabda) and is delimited by the relation of substratumhood (āśrayatva)—exists in the individual cow (go) by means of the relation of its own qualificandhood; it exists in the universal cowness (gotva) by means of the relation of its own qualificandhood as delimited by the delimitorhood (avacchedakatva) residing in the delimitorhood of the relation of inherence (samavāya), which is itself delimited by the relation of inherence; and it exists in inherence by means of the relation of the delimitorhood of the delimitorhood residing in the delimitorhood of the relationhood (saṃsargatā) as delimited by its own qualifierhood.
Thus, the individual cow, the universal cowness, and inherence are the denotata (vācyāḥ) of the word "cow."

Now, regarding that very same position of denotativeness (*vācakatva*): denotativeness consists in possessing a relation characterized by being a qualifier (*prakāratā*)—which is itself characterized by being a qualifier residing in the objectness (*viṣayatā*) delimited by the relation of being the locus qualified by the meaning (*arthaviśiṣṭāśrayatva*), which in turn is delimited by objectness residing in the cognition (*bodha*) characterized by being a qualifier delimited by the qualificandumness (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the cognition, which is further characterized by being a qualifier delimited by the qualificandumness residing in the state of being produced (*janyatva*). Alternatively, denotativeness is the possession of such a qualifier as it resides in the convention (*saṅketa*).

The qualification of the object (*arthavaiśiṣṭya*) resides in the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) delimited by the relation of substratum-ness (*āśrayatva*) which is itself delimited by the state of being the object-domain; this [residence] occurs through one of the following two relations: (1) being delimited by the qualifierhood that is itself delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) as delimited by the deliminatorhood (*avacchedakatva*) residing in its own [the qualifierhood's] own deliminatorhood, which is in turn described by its own deliminatorhood; or (2) being delimited by the qualifierhood residing in the deliminatorhood that describes the deliminatorhood residing in itself.

The word "cow" (go-śabda) is the denoter of the cow, the cowness, and inherence because: the property of being the subject residing in the objecthood produced by the cognition generated by the word [the cow] occurs in the qualifierhood delimited by the relation of substratumhood (*āśrayatva*) with respect to its own resident qualificandumhood (*viśeṣyatā*); cowness occurs with respect to its own resident qualificandumhood by means of the relation of being delimited by the qualifierhood that is itself delimited by that [qualificandumhood]; and inherence occurs by means of the relation of being delimited by the qualifierhood that is itself delimited by the delimitorhood delimited by the relatumhood (*saṃsargatā*) that is itself delimited by the delimitorhood residing in itself. Thus, the word "cow" is the denoter of the cow, cowness, and inherence.

Alternatively, denotability (*vācyatva*) is defined according to the intention "let this word convey this meaning. It is a convention (*saṃketa*) existing in the relation of being the locus of a particularity delimited by a particularity residing in the capacity to produce [cognition], which in turn is determined by a subject-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the word; or rather, denotability is the state of possessing such a subject-ness as is intended by that convention.

In this very context, denotative power (*vācakatva*) is the convention (*saṃketa*), defined by the relation of possessing a qualificandumness (*viśeṣyatā*) that is determined by a subjectness (*prakāratā*) delimited by a residuum residing in a cognition qualified by an object; or alternatively, denotative power is the possession of such a qualificandumness belonging to the convention. In this case, the relation is to be applied in reverse order.

According to the third convention, being denotable (*vācyatva*) consists in the convention being related [to the object] by way of the relation of possessing a subjecthood delimited by "cognition-ness" as determined by a mode residing in "being produced by words"; or, being denotable consists in possessing such a subjecthood belonging to the convention.

Expressiveness (*vācakatva*) according to the third convention consists in the convention’s being related, by way of the relation of being a qualifier delimited by the qualifierhood residing in the state of being produced—which is itself delimited by the state of being produced as qualified by the objective determination (*viśeṣyatā*) delimited by the state of being a cognition qualified by the object—to the convention; or, expressiveness is the possession of such a qualifierhood belonging to the convention.

Now, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is that which possesses the sense organs; inference (*anumāna*) consists of the manifestation (*sphuraṇa*) and so forth; and verbal cognition (*śabdajñāna*) is also the direct perception of the word itself. Through the auxiliary factors of the apprehension of power (*śaktigraha*) and the apprehension of indication (*lakṣaṇāgraha*)—whether by means of the primary function (*śābdīvṛtti*) or by the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) consisting of a relationship with the denotable meaning—the cognition of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārthabodha*) arises as the comprehension of the relation between the heard word and its object, mediated by the recollection of the word-meanings. Thus, according to the father’s conviction, the cognition produced by the mother’s words is the instrument (*karaṇa*), the operation upon that object is the intermediate process (*vyāpāra*), and the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is the result (*phala*). In this regard:

The auxiliary cause for those who possess knowledge of either the denotative power (*śakti*) or the indicative power (*lakṣaṇā*) should be understood as extending as far as verbal usage (*śābdavyavahāra*). A word is "denotative" (*vācaka*) when it brings about the cognition of its expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*); and the cognition of the word is the means for the external usage produced by that [meaning], as well as for the usage indicated by silent verses (*mauniśloka*) and so forth, and even for usages such as the manifestation (*sphuraṇa*) [of the meaning]. And that [cognition of the word] is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

It is universally accepted that the perception of form is the instrument (*karaṇa*)—and thus the cause (*kāraṇa*)—in the perception of a jar, the perception of smoke in the perception of fire, and the perception of sound in verbal cognition. Even for those who disagree [on other matters], this is indeed established by other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the identification of one's father. Furthermore, the sciences of logic (*ānvīkṣikī*), the three Vedas (*trayī*), economics (*vārtā*), and statecraft (*daṇḍanīti*), as well as matters pertaining to the world beyond, are exclusively to be understood through the science of words (*śabdaśāstra*). The injunction "one's own Veda is to be studied" establishes that the means of valid knowledge are exclusively to be understood through the science of words.

The injunction "one's own Veda should be studied" establishes the authority of verbal testimony (*śabda*). All branches of phonetics (*śikṣā*) consist of sound. Poetry has sound as its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The systems of government and justice have sound as their means of valid cognition. The legal practices of people from different regions depend upon the meaning of words and language. The legal practices regarding injunctions and prohibitions depend upon the meaning of words and language. The scripture, which is primarily concerned with injunctions, prohibitions, and so forth, has sound as its means of valid cognition. That which pertains to one's motherland is essentially composed of the mother tongue.

The science of music (*saṅgīta-śāstra*) is based on the system of sound. Grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is the authority regarding words. The syllable *oṃ* is an eternal word that serves as an authority. Speech that corresponds to reality is authoritative. The power of words subsists through primary denotation (*śakti*) and secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). When perception or inference is obstructed in various instances, the employment of words therein is the primary means for the fruit of understanding the meaning. The aesthetic flavors (*rasa*), ornaments (*alaṃkāra*), and so forth of poetry are to be known through words. Mantras connected with deities and sacrificial materials are authoritative. Since the Veda has action as its purpose, those parts which do not have that as their purpose are useless.

Because they form a single syntactical unit with the injunction (*vidhi*), [the mantras] serve the purpose of praising those injunctions. The Sāmaveda consists of praise and is a means of valid knowledge (*śabdapramāṇa*). The relationship between word and meaning is eternal; like speech and its object, they are joined together. For the sake of mutual recognition among the masculine, feminine, and neuter genders of words according to their forms, the means of valid knowledge consisting of sound is employed. The traditional collection of phonemes (*akṣarasamāmnāya*), which is the mass of Brahman, is the authority. The instruction of the letters is for the purpose of achieving the desired cognition.

One should not employ a word that lacks a grammatical base (*apada*). Regarding the fourteen aphorisms (*sūtra*), which consist of both the imitator and the imitated, both difference and non-difference are authoritative. Within the traditional collection of aphorisms (*sūtrasamāmnāya*), the lineage of Maheśvara is authoritative. [Examples of such words include: "vṛddhir ādaic," "akāro vāsudevaḥ," "om ity ekākṣaraṃ brahma," and "atha" as an auspicious term; these are authoritative words that serve as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). (Verses 472–478)

[The meaning of a word is determined] through grammatical derivation, analogy, lexicons, the words of reliable authorities, usage, the remainder of a sentence, explicit explanation, and established convention. (479)

The apprehension of the expressive power [of words] arises from context, from association with purposeful activity, from the result, and from repeated practice; furthermore, there is both valid cognition and error.

Grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is also a means of grasping word-potency (*śakti*): for instance, [it teaches] that verbal roots such as *bhū* have their own meanings, such as "existence" (*sattā*); that in words like *pācaka*, the *kṛt*-suffix has the sense of the agent; that particles (*nipāta*) such as *vipūya* have meanings like "muñja-grass"; that bases (*prakṛti*) have their respective meanings; that suffixes such as *laṭ* in the rule "the suffix *laṭ* occurs in the present tense" have the meaning of the present time; that the verb (*ākhyāta*) has the sense of the agent; and that case-endings (*vibhakti*) have the sense of the substratum (*āśraya*), among other things—wherein the second, third, and seventh cases have the sense of the substratum, specifically the second case.

The apprehension of the expressive power (*śaktigraha*) occurs as follows: in the case of an action that is the locus of the fruit produced by it, [the power of] the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is apprehended; in the case of the agent, who is the locus of the operation denoted by the verbal root, [the power of] the first person is apprehended; in the case of the locus, [the power of] the seventh case (*saptamī*); in the case of the limit (*avadhi*), [the power of] the fifth case (*pañcamī*); in the case of the recipient (*sampradāna*) intended for the purpose of the action, [the power of] the fourth case (*caturthī*); in the case of the relation (*sambandha*), [the power of] the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*); in the case of singularity and so forth, [the power of] suffixes such as *su*; and in the case of specific meanings, [the power of] formations such as compounds (*samāsa*).

In some cases, [the Naiyāyikas hold that] the denotation of verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*) is effort (*kṛti*); [they hold that] after transitive roots, when followed by *ya*-class suffixes and so forth, the verbal suffixes denote the agent, whereas when not followed by *ya*-class suffixes, those suffixes are devoid of meaning. The Naiyāyikas maintain that the verbal suffix has the power (*śakti*) to denote effort; the nine new Grammarians (*navīna-vaiyākaraṇas*) maintain that both the agentive and objective verbal suffixes have the power to denote merely the substratum (*āśraya*). The particle *eva* functions to exclude connection with another (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*), to exclude non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*), or to exclude absolute non-connection (*atyantāyoga-vyavaccheda*). The particle *iva* functions to denote similarity (*sādṛśya*).

The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the denotative power (*śakti*) of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) resides in the operation (*vyāpāra*), while in certain cases there is a conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhā lakṣaṇā*). The author of the *Cintāmaṇi* holds that the verbal suffix has a conventional metaphorical indication in its sense of the substratum (*āśrayatva*). The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the meaning of the verbal suffix is the productive urge (*bhāvanā*). In the case of "he desires" (*icchati*), the verbal suffix has a metaphorical indication in the sense of the substratum; in "he strives" (*yatate*), it is in the sense of the substratum; and in "he perishes" (*naśyati*), the verbal suffix has a metaphorical indication in the sense of the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*). The author of the *Ratnakośa* maintains that the verbal suffix has its denotative power in the act of bringing about (*utpādanā*).

Now, from analogy—that is, from the perception of similarity residing in a *gavaya* as determined by a cow—the apprehension of the denotative power (*śakti*) arises that "the *gavaya* is the denotation of the word *gavaya*. According to the Grammarian (*Vaiyākaraṇa*) school, verbal cognition has the meaning of the verbal root as its primary qualificand; for example, in "Look, the deer runs," the cognition is: "The act of seeing performed by you has as its object the running performed by the deer. In "He cooks," the cognition is: "Cooking is the object of the operation. According to the Mīmāṃsaka school, verbal cognition has the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) as its primary qualificand; for example, in "Devadatta cooks rice," [the cognition is]: "The cooking has Devadatta as its agent."

"Odanabhāvyikā devadattakṛtiḥ" (The act of Devadatta is that which has cooked rice as its object). According to the Naiyāyika view, verbal cognition has the nominative case-ending as its primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣya*). For example, in "Caitra cooks rice" (*caitras taṇḍulān pacati*), the cognition is: "Caitra possesses an effort conducive to the cooking residing in the rice. Through the relation of difference (*bhedānvaya*), "Caitra’s wealth" (*caitrasya dhanam*) means "wealth whose ownership is characterized by [residing in] Caitra. Through the relation of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*), "the blue pot" (*nīlo ghaṭaḥ*) means "a pot non-different from the blue."

The acquisition of the word-meaning (śaktigraha) for the term *acyuta* occurs as "the one with yellow garments from his treasury" (*kośāt-pītāmbara*) and "the wielder of the Śārṅga bow" (*śārṅga*) in reference to Śrī Kṛṣṇa; whereas for the term *nīla*, there is the acquisition of the meaning as the color blue (*nīlarūpa*), as that which is qualified by blue (*nīlaviśiṣṭa*), or the primary denotation (*śakti*) resides in the color blue while it is indicated (*lakṣaṇā*) in that which is qualified by blue.

An authoritative person (*āpta*) is one who knows the truth regarding the application [of words]. From the statement uttered by such a person—based on the worldly usage that "the cuckoo is denoted by the word *pika*"—and having observed a child's action of bringing a jar after hearing the command "Bring the jar," and noting that this action of bringing the jar was preceded by an inclination to act, which in turn was produced by a cognition, [the child concludes]: "The cognition of the jar-bringing is produced by the sentence 'Bring the jar,' because it follows the presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that sentence. Thus, he grasps the expressive power (*śakti*) of the word as residing in the jar as qualified by the action.

From that, the apprehension of the word’s power (*śaktigraha*) occurs in other sentences as well by means of that same method. The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the power (*śakti*) is twofold: denotative (*smārikā*) and productive of experience (*ānubhāvikī*). For the word *ghaṭa*, the denotative power resides in the universal *ghaṭatva* (pot-ness), while for words such as *paśu* (animal) and others, it resides in the individual (*vyakti*). However, the productive power resides in the pot as conjoined with an action (*kriyānvita-ghaṭa*), and this is simply the will (*icchā*) itself, existing as its own nature. As for verbal roots (*dhātu*), however, their function is to serve as the cause for the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) of a pot conjoined with an action.

The optative (*liṅ*), imperative (*loṭ*), infinitive (*tavya*), and so forth, are the motivators for a verbal cognition associated with "taskness" (*kāryatā*); therefore, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) possess authority by virtue of being syntactically connected with injunctive sentences. In the Nyāya school, words have their denotative power (*śakti*) in their own primary meaning, setting aside "taskness. The Bhaṭṭas maintain that the power of words lies in a meaning conjoined with another. The Naiyāyikas hold that the power resides in the meaning as conjoined, but not in the isolated meaning alone. The Vedāntins also maintain that the power resides in the conjoined meaning.

From the *vākyaśeṣa* (complementary statement): "The sacrificial pap (*caru*) made of barley"—the cognition arises that "becoming a sacrificial pap which is a modification of barley is the means to achieve the desired end," based on the complementary statement, "They remain unsatisfied [only] when there are long-awned [barley grains]. The word *hari* has a denotative power (*śakti*) toward multiple meanings. From *vivaraṇa* (explanation/paraphrase): "There is a jar" is paraphrased as "there is a pot" (*kalaśa*); "he cooks" is paraphrased as "he performs cooking. Thus, the verb root (*ākhyāta*) has the meaning of effort (*yatna*). From association with well-known words: in the sentence "the *pika* sings in the *sahakāra* tree," the denotative power of the word *pika* refers to the *kokila* (cuckoo), by virtue of the contextual force of the mango tree (*āmravṛkṣa*). These are the means for grasping denotative power (*śaktigrahopāya*).

In the case of the command "Bring the Saindhava to the battle," the capacity [of the word] refers to the horse due to the context (*prakaraṇa*). Or, when the meaning is "forgiving an offense together with a gesture from the corner of a cruel eye, having taken a fine of goods," either the capacity (*śakti*) or *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is understood. The capacity for running away in fear, crying out, and so forth, serves as the indicator of the arrival [of danger]. The apprehension of the word's capacity as stated occurs after the direct perception of the result. Alternatively, through repeated practice or the practice of words, the apprehension of the capacity regarding its specific meaning occurs.

Through repeated practice, or through the practice of words, the apprehension of the power [of a word] with respect to its specific meaning arises, as in the case of the Vedānta. The genus (*jāti*), the configuration (*ākṛti*), and the individual (*vyakti*) are the denotable meanings (*śakya*). In the case of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the seed is either the incompatibility of the syntactic connection (*anvayānupapatti*) or the incompatibility of the intended meaning (*tātparyānupapatti*).

The word *tat* has its denotative power (*śakti*) in the mode of a cognition present to the mind; the words *idam* and *etad* have their power in the mode of a perceptual cognition; the word *adas* has its power in the mode of a non-perceptual (remote) cognition; the word *kim* has its power in that which is unspecified yet desired to be known—as in "What is the pot?", where the pot is the object of one's desire to know; and the word *sarva* has its power in pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) qualified by [the property] specified as the delimitor of the subjecthood (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), specifically in the pervasiveness residing in the delimitor of the predicatehood (*vidheyatāvacchedaka*).

"All pots possess color"—that is, "pots are those which possess color, which pervades the property of being a pot. The word *tvaṃ* (the second person pronoun) has its denotative power (*śakti*) directed toward the independent speaker at that particular time; the word *eva* has its power directed toward that which is qualified by exclusivity (*kaivalya*), meaning that which is characterized by the absence of a second similar entity; the word *dhenu* has its power directed toward a single substratum (*dharmin*) qualified by both the state of being the object of milking and the property of being a cow. In these cases, because the power is one and the same, there is no polysemy (*nānārthatā*). However, in the case of words such as *hari*, the power is distinct with respect to individuals qualified by distinct properties.

The word (*pada*) is denotative (*śakta*), whereas the sentence (*vākya*) is indicative (*lākṣaṇika*). The word is of four kinds: that possessing the power of etymological derivation (*yoga-śaktimat*), that possessing the power of conventional usage (*ruḍhi-śaktimat*), that possessing the single power of both derivation and convention (*yoga-ruḍhy-eka-śaktimat*), and that possessing a power distinct from both the derivative and conventional meanings (*yogārtha-ruḍhārtha-bhinna-śaktimat*). An example of a word possessing the power of derivation is *pācaka* ("cook") and the like; the meaning produced by the power of its constituent parts—namely the root *pac* and the suffix *ṇvul*—is "the agent of cooking. Derivative words (*yaugika*) are threefold: compounds (*samāsa*), those ending in secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), and those ending in primary suffixes (*kṛdanta*). Even a copulative compound (*dvandva*) is derivative. Words such as *brāhmaṇī*, *śvaśrū*, and *śūdrā* are derivative.

Yaugikatva (derivational status) is the state of possessing a collection [of phonemes] that lacks the property of being the delimitor of the capacity [to denote a meaning] as a whole. A word is *yaugika* with respect to a particular meaning if it possesses such a sequence [of phonemes] (*ānupūrvī*) which, delimited by its own constituent parts alone, serves as the delimitor of the generative capacity (*janakatā*) for a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) regarding that specific qualified object, by way of being its objective content (*viṣayatā*). For example, the word *go* (cow), as in *gomaṇḍala* (a herd of cows), is *yaugika* with respect to the meaning "one who goes," because it is derived from the root *gam* with the suffix *ḍoḥ* according to the rule *gamer ḍoḥ*, and thus possesses the meaning of its constituents, namely, the state of being an agent of motion (*gamanakartṛtva*). The word *go* is thus like the word *go* [in the compound *gomaṇḍala*].

*Maṇḍala* means a circumference; *maṇḍapa*, however, is [the word for] a canopy by convention (*ruḍhi*). Conventionality (*rūḍhatva*) consists in possessing a collection of properties that serve as the delimiters of the capacity [to denote] that which is not formed by etymological derivation (*pajā’ghaṭita-śaktatāvacchedaka-samudāyatvavattvam*). Convention is threefold: based on a cause (*naimittika*), technical (*pāribhāṣika*), and based on a limiting condition (*aupādhika*). Alternatively, convention is fourfold, consisting of designations based on genus (*jāti*), substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*spanda*).

The conventional meaning (rūḍhatva) of a word with respect to a certain object is its being a word possessing such a sequence [of phonemes]—while being distinct from that which is both etymological (yoga) and conventional (ruḍha)—which serves as the delimiting factor for the objectivity of a desire whose mode consists in generating a cognition of that specific object, as seen in the case of *go* and *gavaya* etc. by the class-property *gotva* (cowness), *paśu* and *aḍhya* etc. by the tail and wealth etc., *dhanya* and *piśuna* etc. by merit and malice etc., and *cala* and *capala* etc. by their respective actions.

The word *paṅkaja* (mud-born) is both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍha*). By the power of its parts—namely, "that which is born from mud" (*paṅkāj jāyate*)—and by the power of the whole through convention, it conveys the lotus as a composite entity. Knowledge of the conventional meaning acts as an obstacle to the knowledge of the purely etymological meaning. Alternatively, because words denoting individuals refer to the specific instance present [in context], and because the connection of the part-meaning with the whole-meaning is stronger due to its proximity, when the conventional meaning is sublated, secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs for the sake of the white water-lily (*kumuda*) due to the impossibility of syntactic connection otherwise.

Where there is the intended meaning (tātparya) and the sublation of anything other than that, there the term is etymological (yaugika). However, in the case of "paṅkaja" [mud-born], the meaning "land-lotus" is obtained through secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) due to the impossibility of syntactic connection (anvayānupapatti). When there is no sublation of the meanings of the individual components, there is no secondary signification due to the impossibility of syntactic connection; rather, it is an etymological power (śakti). But in the case of "sthalapadma," there is non-abandonment of the primary sense (ajahatsvārthā) secondary signification due to the impossibility of the intended meaning (tātparyānupapatti).

Now, regarding compounds (*samāsa*): examples include *kṛṣṇasarpa* and the like; those ending in secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) such as *vāsudeva*; and those ending in primary suffixes (*kṛt*) such as *paṅkaja*. A name with a particular sequence of phonemes is "etymologically-figurative" (*yogarūḍha*) with respect to a certain meaning if that meaning is constituted by that [etymological] meaning, provided that the state of being a delimiting factor for the production of a relational cognition—wherein the object is a property belonging to a certain meaning residing in its own substratum and the qualifier is a certain meaning presented by a function residing in a constituent part of its own substratum—is delimited by that very sequence of phonemes.

The nature of being *yogarūḍha* (etymological-conventional) consists in possessing that state of being a composite whole which includes a word capable of denoting a property delimited by a feature co-located with the delimitor of the conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakyatāvacchedaka*). This [delimitor] is the delimitor of the capacity to denote the conventional sense (*rūḍhi-śakti-nirūpakatāvacchedaka*).

Now, words such as *udbhid*, *mahārajata*, *maṇḍapa*, and *yakṣakardama*—by virtue of the power of their constituent parts (*avayavaśakti*)—convey the etymological meanings of "tree and shrub," "great silver," "one who makes a pavilion," and "the paste of Yakṣas. However, they do not convey the conventional meanings of "sacrifice," "gold," "canopy," and "sandalwood" as separate, established senses. This is because the etymological meaning and the conventional meaning are understood independently of one another.

That which is composed of words whose locus of delimitorhood is delimited by a relation that is the objective-condition (viṣayatā) determined by the causal-condition (kāraṇatā) residing in cognition, which in turn is determined by the effect-condition (kāryatā) residing in verbal comprehension (śābdabodha) characterized by an objective-condition delimited by the delimitor of the conventional power (rūḍhi-śakyatāvacchedaka); and [that which is] such that its locus of delimitorhood is delimited by a relation that is the objective-condition determined by the causal-condition residing in cognition, which is determined by the effect-condition residing in verbal comprehension characterized by an objective-condition delimited by a property non-co-located with the delimitor of the conventional power.

The status of being a composite whole (*samudāyatva*), the state of possessing that [meaning] (*tadvattva*), and the nature of being both etymological and conventional (*yaugika-ruḍhatva*) [are the definitions of a word]. However, in the general causal relation between the knowledge of power (*śakti*) and verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), the power residing in the relation (*saṃsarga*) must necessarily be acknowledged. Since the verbal cognition of two word-meanings—which are themselves easily graspable—is untenable without their mutual connection (*anvaya*), and since that connection is unavoidable for the sake of accounting for the cognition of what is otherwise ungraspable, let there be power (*śakti*) in every case [of the relation] as well. This is because the fact that the connection between word-meanings is invariably determined by the knowledge of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is accepted as primary, and thus the connection is admitted to be within the scope of the power.

The causes of verbal cognition (*śābda*) are distinct from the causes of inference, as is the *parikara* (auxiliary factors). The apprehension of word-potency (*śaktigraha*) is distinct from the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāptigraha*); the hearing of a sentence is distinct from the perception of a logical mark (*liṅgadarśana*); the recollection of word-meanings is distinct from the recollection of pervasion; the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence is distinct from inferential cognition; the cognition of word-meanings is distinct from the cognition of the probandum and the subject (*sādhyapakṣapratīti*); the relations of potency (*śakti*), indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and suggestion (*vyañjanā*) are distinct from the relation of pervasion; and the ascertainment of being spoken by a reliable person (*āptoktatvaniścaya*) is distinct from [the requirements of] presence in the subject (*pakṣasattva*) and so forth.

The verbal cognition is distinct from the conventional designation because its object is pervasion (*vyāpti*); it is distinct from inference because of the difference in their respective after-cognitions (*anuvyavasāya*); and the valid knowledge of the meanings recalled by words possessing expectancy, proximity, and compatibility is distinct from the inferential knowledge established by the inference whose subject (*pakṣa*) consists of the word and its meaning.

In an inference based on the "winged-foot" (padapakṣaka) model, the knowledge of the logical mark (*liṅga*) is useful; in such inference, the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) regarding the nature of the reason (*hetu*) is useful only when it is known. In verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), however, expectancy is a cause by its very existence (*svarūpasatī*). Therefore, since the relation (*saṃsarga*) is not established through inference, verbal testimony (*śabda*) as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is indispensable. Expectancy is defined as the desire to know the meanings of words as recalled by the words uttered in proximity (*samabhivyāhṛta*). Just like Vedic speech, worldly speech (*laukika-śabda*) is also a means of valid knowledge; the court of justice, possessing state authority and attested by worldly utterances, is a means of valid knowledge.

The comprehension of the true nature of supersensuous objects is rooted in verbal testimony (*śabda*). Where perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) are sublated, knowledge based on verbal testimony is the valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*); likewise, the extraordinary knowledge of the sages (*ārṣajñāna*) is rooted in scripture (*āgama*). Regarding the certain determination of an object situated inside a house, it is the power of verbal testimony alone that functions as the valid cognition. In the direct realization of Brahman (*brahmasākṣātkāra*), hearing (*śravaṇa*) is the cause. Through its function, verbal testimony nourishes *vyañjanā* (suggestion).

Verbal comprehension occurs through the denotative function (*abhidhā*) by means of the mind assisted by memory; verbal comprehension occurs through the indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*) by means of the mind assisted by memory; likewise, there is the comprehension of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) through the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*). Therefore, the function of suggestion is indispensable. Since there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the word and the suggested meanings, verbal testimony (*śabda-pramāṇa*) is not the primary means of knowledge therein; rather, in the cognition of the suggested meaning, the word is merely the instrument (*karaṇa*).

Regarding Brahman, the Upanishads serve as the authoritative source for various philosophical systems; regarding the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), sacrifices, and so forth, the authority belongs to those Vedic texts whose conclusions have been established by the Mīmāṃsā Śāstra. Thus, verbal testimony (*śabdapramāṇa*) encompasses the entirety of literature in its various forms. The Veda is the authority for the state of liberation, as in the text: "He does not return again. All worldly and Vedic statements possess validity by virtue of generating knowledge that removes doubt concerning their respective specific objects.

From words, there arises indirect knowledge consisting of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). The seven literary principles residing within verbal expression—namely, indication (*lakṣaṇā*), ornament (*alaṃkāra*), quality (*guṇa*), defect (*doṣa*), style (*rīti*), suggestion (*dhvani*), and aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)—are authoritative, nourished by valid means of knowledge, and productive of verbal cognition.

The Veda is the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), being a collection of words that is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*). The word "Veda" is both conventional (*rūḍha*) and etymological-conventional (*yogarūḍha*); the terms "Brāhmaṇa" and "Upaniṣad" are purely etymological (*yaugika*). It is called *Ṛk* because by it the gods are praised (*ṛcyante stūyante devā anayā*); *Sāman* because it pacifies sin (*syati pāpam*); and *Yajus* because by it one sacrifices (*ijyate 'nena*)—these are etymological designations. It is also etymologically defined as "Veda" because by it one knows dharma (*vidanti anena dharmam iti vedah*). The term *om* is conventional, yet it is also etymological when analyzed into its three phonemes. *Ātharvaṇa* refers to the collection of the Atharvans; it is conventional for the mantras of the Atharvans, while "Atharvan" is a name for a powerful son of Aṅgiras.

Now, bases such as *ghaṭa*, *paṭa*, and *pācaka* are capable of denoting their own referents; suffixes such as *sup* and *tiṅ* are [suffixes]; *sup*-suffixes and the like are capable of denoting objecthood (*karmatva*), agenthood (*kartṛtva*), and so forth; *tiṅ*-suffixes and the like are capable of denoting being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), effort (*kṛti*), present time (*vartamānatva*), singularity (*ekatva*), and so forth; particles (*nipāta*) such as *ca*, *vā*, and *ha* are respectively capable of denoting conjunction (*samuccaya*), option (*vikalpa*), clarity (*sphuṭatva*), and so forth. [The suffix] *su* occurs in the sense of singularity. Bases such as *ghaṭa*, *paṭa*, and *pācaka* necessarily require the assistance of a case-ending (*vibhakti*), while suffixes such as *sup* and the like necessarily [require a base].

By virtue of its cooperation with the *prakṛti* (base), and because particles (*nipāta*) such as *ca*, *vā*, and others invariably generate the cognition of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) through the cooperation of elided case-endings and the like, meaningful words (*sārthaka-śabda*) are threefold: *prakṛti*, *pratyaya* (suffix), and *nipāta*. Even though [a compound like] "hare's horn" (*śaśaviṣāṇa*) is logically impossible, there is no defect in its being considered meaningful, because since the hare and the horn are each well-known individually, it can produce a cognition through a relation other than the relation of being produced (*janyatva*), namely, the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Thus, it possesses the status of being meaningful (*sārthakatva*).

The *vikaraṇa* suffixes such as *śyan* and *śnā*, the augments (*āgama*) such as *num*, the substitutes (*ādeśa*) such as *vas*, and even words like *nibha*, *nikaṣa*, and *sādi*—all of which convey meanings similar to the original base—are dependent upon the verbal root (*prakṛti*). They possess the meaning of the preceding root and so forth; they function through other operations or consist of their own operations. Being recognized as linguistic units (*śabda*), otherwise, due to the non-expressiveness of the rule (*sūtra*) that establishes them, they would not even achieve the status of being derived words (*śabda-niṣpanna*). Ultimately, they must be considered as possessing inherent power by virtue of their own nature.

In the singular, *su*; in the dual, *au*; in the plural, *jas*—these are capable [of expressing number]. In the vocative (*sambodhana*), *śaktaḥ* [is used]. The suffix *ṭāp* is the domain for the intention to express femininity. The *l*-suffixes beginning with *laṭ* are capable of expressing both the object and the agent when derived from transitive roots; however, from intransitive roots, they are capable of expressing only the state (*bhāva*) and the agent. Nevertheless, by the rule "in the present tense, *laṭ*" (*vartamāne laṭ*), there is an apprehension of the capacity of the *laṭ* suffixes to denote the present time; yet, by the force of the rule "the *l*-suffixes [denote] the object and the agent, and [the state] after intransitives" (*laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ*), the verbal suffixes beginning with *tip* denote the agent.

The apprehension of power (*śaktigraha*): the apprehension of power in the case of case-endings (*vibhakti*) regarding meanings such as locus (*āśraya*), limit (*avadhi*), intended recipient (*uddeśya*), and relation (*sambandha*). Specifically, for the second, third, and seventh cases: the second case has power with respect to the locus; the second case has power with respect to the object (*karman*), which is the locus of the result produced by the action; the third case has power with respect to the agent (*kartṛ*), which is the locus of the activity denoted by the verbal root (*dhātvartha-vyāpāra*); the seventh case has power with respect to the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), based on the rule "the substratum is the locus" (*ādhāro'dhikaraṇam*); the fifth case has power with respect to the limit (*avadhi*), based on the rule "that from which there is movement away is the point of departure" (*dhruvamapāye'pādānam*); and the fourth case has power with respect to the intended recipient (*uddeśya*), based on the rule "whom one intends through the action, that is the recipient" (*karmaṇā yamabhipraiti sa sampradānam*).

The apprehension of the expressive power (*śakti*) regarding the genitive case is as follows: "the genitive is used for the recipient" (*sampradāne*) and "the genitive is used for the remainder" (*ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe*). Regarding the suffixes beginning with *su* (the nominal endings), there is an apprehension of expressive power in respect to singularity and so forth. In the case of "Maitra exists" (*maitro'sti*), the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is the locus (*āśrayatva*). In "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), the meaning of the verbal suffix is being a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). In "it is stayed" (*sthīyate*), the meaning of the verbal suffix is the present time (*vartamānatva*). In "cook" (*pācakaḥ*), the suffix *kṛt* has its expressive power in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) within its own meaning. In "Kāśyapi" (*kāśyapiḥ*), the suffix has its expressive power in the sense of a descendant (*apatya*) delimited by Kaśyapa within its own meaning.

The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the general verbal suffix (*lā*) has the power (*śakti*) to denote mere operation (*vyāpāra*). The Naiyāyikas hold that there is a conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) of the verbal suffix in the sense of operation. However, the author of the *Cintāmaṇi* (Gangeśa) maintains that there is a conventional metaphorical indication of the verbal suffix in the sense of substratum (*āśrayatva*). The Mīmāṃsakas further argue that in the expression "he knows" (*jānāti*), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is knowledge delimited by "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*), while the meaning of the verbal suffix is "productive activity" (*bhāvanā*) or "causing to arise. Thus, the resulting cognition is: "one who possesses the production of a knowledge whose substratum is cognizedness."

In the expression "naśyati" (perishes), there is a conventional secondary signification (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) regarding the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) as denoting the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*); the resulting cognition is that "there is one jar which is the counter-correlate of destruction. The author of the *Ratnakośa*, however, maintains that the verbal suffix has the power (*śakti*) to denote productive activity (*bhāvanā*) or production (*utpādanā*). The meaning of the verbal root is the producer of the meaning of the verbal suffix. For example: "he cooks" means he produces cooking; "he goes" means he produces going; "he exerts effort" means he produces effort. In this context, the verbal suffix has the meaning of the locus (*āśrayatā*). The perfect tense suffix (*liṭ*) possesses the power to denote the past, non-recent, and non-indirect (non-perceptual) time.

The suffix *luṭ* has the power [to denote] a future sense not pertaining to the current day; *laṭ* has the power [to denote] a general future sense; *loṭ* has the power [to denote] injunctions and so forth; *liṅ* and *loṭ* have the power [to denote] benediction; *laṅ* has the power [to denote] a past sense not pertaining to the current day; *liṅ* has the power [to denote] injunction, invitation, permission, request, inquiry, and entreaty; *luṅ* has the power [to denote] a past sense; verbal roots (*dhātu*) have the power [to denote] their respective meanings; the suffix *ṇic* has the power [to denote] the meaning to be expressed as instigation, entreaty, consent, instruction, and so forth; and the suffix *san* has the power [to denote] desire.

Furthermore, the suffix *yaṅ* has the power to express repetition and intensity. *Kyac* is capable of expressing desire. *Kyaṅ* and *kāmyac* have the power to express longing (*lālasā*). *Kyaṅ* is used in the sense of behaving like someone or something (*ācāra*). Thus, the suffixes produced through the process of nominal derivation (*nāmadhātu*) possess multiple powers and convey meanings appropriate to the root-meaning. When a verbal suffix (*sārvadhātuka*) expresses a state or action (*bhāva-kriyā*), the suffix *yak* occurs; therein, the *lakāra* (verbal root marker) is merely a restatement (*anuvādaka*). In the case of the *lakāra* expressing a state, there is the singular number of the first person (*uttamaikatva*); the state is expressed by the *tiṅ* suffix, as is the attainment of singularity.

Where the action itself (*karman*) is intended to be expressed as the agent (*kartṛ*), there the verbal suffixes (*lakāra*) are used in the sense of the agent or the state (*bhāva*); for example, *gaur payo dugdhe svayam eva*, meaning "the cow itself releases the milk. *Udumbaraḥ phalaṃ pacyate*, meaning "the udumbara tree ripens its fruit at the [proper] time. When a word that awakens memory (*smṛtibodhinī*) is the attendant word (*upapada*), the suffix *lṛṭ* is used for the past not of today; optionally, *laṅ*; and *liṭ* in the case of something beyond the range of sight. *Liṭ* is used for absolute concealment. When the matter is being questioned, *laṅ* and *liṭ* are used where *liṅ* would otherwise apply. For the past not of today, *laṭ* is used.

When the sense to be expressed is one of inquiry within the scope of the *liṅ* (optative), the *laṅ* (imperfect) and *liṭ* (perfect) may be used. For the past non-current time (*bhūtānadyatana*), the *laṭ* (present) is used; for the past in general, the *laṭ* is used when joined with *purā*. When joined with the particles *yāvat* or *purā*, the *laṭ* is used in the sense of the past non-current time. With the words *kadā* or *karhi*, the *laṭ* is optionally used. For the sense of proximity to the present, the suffixes expressing the present tense are expressive. In the expression of hope regarding the future, the suffixes of the past and present are capable [of being used]. When a synonym of "quickly" (*kṣipra*) is employed as an adjunct, the *lṛṭ* (periphrastic future) is used. In the statement of a wish (*āśaṃsā*), the *liṅ* is used. The *liṅ* is used to express cause and effect (*hetu-hetumat*). The *liṅ* and *loṭ* (imperative) are used in the sense of desire.

The optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used for meanings of desire when the agent is the same; it is also used for injunction, invitation, and so forth. The kṛtya suffixes denote the meanings of command, injunction, permission, and the arrival of the proper time. In that regard, the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) is also used. The kṛtya suffixes and the suffix *tṛc* are used in the sense of "deserving," as is the optative suffix. The optative suffix and the kṛtya suffixes are also used in the sense of "capability. When the action denoted by the verbal ending is subordinate, the suffixes are expressive [of the relation] with a root expressing a secondary action, and in other cases as well. The imperative suffix is used for frequency and intensity.

In secondary application (*anuprayoga*), the suffixes beginning with *laṭ* and those beginning with *tiP* function according to their respective roles to indicate number, tense, and person. This [usage], however, has as its intended meaning (*tātparya*) a relation of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*). The suffixes *kṛtya*, *kta*, and those having the sense of *khal* denote both the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). The suffixes *tavyat*, *tavya*, and *anīyar* denote the abstract action—that is, the meaning of the verbal root—and are employed for the grammatical correctness (*śabdasādhutva*) of the word. In that context, the default (*autsargika*) is the singular number and the neuter gender. The suffix *kelimara* is used in the sense of the abstract action and the object. The suffix *kelimara* is also used in the sense of the object. The suffix *tavyat* is used after the root *vas* in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).

The *kṛtya* suffixes and *luṭ* are used to express the objects of engagement (*pravṛtti*) or non-engagement (*apravṛtti*), such as impermanence (*anityatva*) and so forth. The suffix *anīyar* is applied to the root *snā* in the sense of an instrument; *anīyar* is applied to the root *dā* in the sense of tradition (*sampradāya*). After the root *upalabh*, the augment *num* is added when expressing praise; after the root *ācāra*, the suffix *yat* is applied in senses other than "teacher. The suffix *yat* and words ending in *yat* are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) in their respective meanings. From the root *bhū*, the suffix *kyap* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*); in the case of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), it is without the augment *iṭ*. The suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the sense of what is inevitable (*avaśyambhāvin*). In forms such as *bhavyaḥ* and *geyaḥ*, the suffix *yat* denotes the agent (*kartṛ*).

In *pravacanīya* and similar forms, the suffix *anīyar* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). In *āplāvya*, the suffix *ṇyat* is used in the sense of the agent. In *sūryaḥ*, the suffix *kyap* is added to the root *sṛ* in the sense of the agent. In *kṛṣṭapacyāḥ*, the suffix *kyap* is used in the sense of the object-agent (*karmakartari*). In *amāvasyā*, the suffix *ṇyat* is added to the root *vas* preceded by the prefix *amā* in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). From the root *ci*, the form *cityaḥ* is derived with the suffix *ṇyat* in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*), along with the augment *tuk*. The suffix *vun* is used in the sense of a benediction (*āśīrvāda*). With the words *go* and *pā* as co-occurring objects (*upapada*), the suffix *ṭak* is applied in the sense of the object. In *puṣpāharaḥ*, the suffix *ac* is used in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*). The suffix *ḍa* is used in the sense of the locus; the suffix *ḍa* is also used in the sense of a benediction; and the suffix *ṭak* is used in the sense of expressing capability (*śakti*).

The suffix *ṇini* occurs when the habitual nature (*tācchīlya*) is to be expressed. The suffix *ṇini* occurs after the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) in the sense of a completed action (*bhūtārtha*), with the agent (*kartṛ*) as the referent. In the case of *śyenacit* ("one who has piled the fire-altar in the shape of a hawk"), the suffix *kvip* is applied to the roots *sthā* and *ci* when referring to the sacrificial mound (*agnisthaṇḍila*). The suffix *ini* occurs in the past tense when censure (*nindā*) is implied, as in *somavikrayī* ("a seller of Soma"). The suffix *kvanip* occurs after the root *kṛ* (to do/make) in the sense of a completed action. The suffix *ḍa* occurs after the root *jan* (to be born) when forming a proper name (*saṃjñā*). The root *śyaiṅ* (to congeal) is used in the sense of becoming solid (*ghanībhūtārtha*). The suffix *kta* occurs in the sense of the beginning of an action (*ādikarma*) when there is an intention to distinguish it from the mere completion of the action; it occurs with the agent (*kartṛ*), the state (*bhāva*), and the object (*karman*). The suffix *kta* also occurs in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). The suffix *kta* also occurs in the sense of the present (*vartamāna*).

The suffix *kta* occurs after a verbal root denoting a neuter state (*bhāva*) in the sense of unspecified time; *kta* also occurs in the present tense. The suffix *ṅvanip* occurs in the past tense; *kta* occurs in the sense of unspecified time within the past tense; *ḍvanip* occurs in the past tense; *atṛn* occurs in the past tense. In the Vedas, *liṭ* occurs in the past tense. Furthermore, the following suffixes occur when the agent (*kartṛ*) possesses that habit (*tacchīla*), etc.: *cānaś*, *kvip*, *tan*, *āluc*, *iṣṇuc*, *gsnu*, *knun*, *dhinuṇ*, *yuc*, *vuñ*, *ukañ*, *pākan*, *uvarac*. The suffixes *ṣṭran* and *itra* occur in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*).

In the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*), the suffix *na* is added to the root *kṛṣ*; the suffix *asun* is added to the root *aś* in the sense of praise; *asun* is added in the sense of strength; and *asun* is added in the sense of a limb of one’s own body. The *uṇādi* suffixes are applied in the present tense in the sense of a name. The suffix *tumun* is used in the sense of abstract action (*bhāva*). The suffix *ṇvul* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). The suffix *ghañ* is used for a case-role other than the agent, in the sense of abstract action, and also in the sense of the agent. The suffix *ṇvul* is used in the sense of the agent. The suffix *map* is used in the sense of excluding the agent. The suffix *athuc* is used in the sense of abstract action. The suffix *ki* is used in the sense of abstract action and so forth. The suffix *ktin* is used in the feminine gender in the sense of abstract action. The suffix *kyap* is used in the sense of abstract action. The suffix *śa* (which excludes *ghañ*) is used in the sense of abstract action. The suffix *ṇini* is used in the sense of the agent. The suffixes *ktic* and *kti* are used in the sense of a benediction (*āśīrvāda*).
The first case ending is capable of expressing the meaning of the nominal stem itself, as well as gender alone, measure, and number.

The suffixes *ṭāp*, *ṅīp*, and *ṅīṣ* are used when femininity (*strītva*) is to be expressed; *vun* is used in the sense of a blessing (*āśīrvāda*); *nuk* is used in the sense of pregnancy (*garbha-saṃyoga*) or union with a husband (*bhartṛ-saṃyoga*). The suffix *cāp* is used in the sense of a deity (*devatā*), as in *sūryā*. The suffix *ṅīṣ* is used in its own sense (*svārtha*), as in *ānuk* for *kṣatriyāṇī*. When denoting a genus (*jāti*) and expressing femininity, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. The suffix *ūṅ* is used when femininity is to be expressed. The suffixes *ṅīna* and *ti* are also used when expressing femininity. Now, regarding meanings prior to "divine" (*prāg-dīvyatīya*), there are the suffixes *aṇ*, *ṇya*, *añ*, *nañ*, and *snañ*. For the meaning of offspring (*apatya*), there is *gotrāpatya*; for the meaning of lineage-offspring (*gotrāpatya*), there is *yañ*; and for meanings prior to "divine," there is *añ*.

The suffix *iñ* is used in the sense of offspring; *a-* for many offspring; *aṇ* for offspring when the progenitor is not a *ṛṣi*; *aṇ*, *ḍhak*, *yat*, and *ṭhak* in the sense of offspring; three [suffixes] in the sense of the base itself (*svārtha*); *phak* and *phañ* in the sense of a lineage (*gotra*); *ḍhak*, *chaṇ*, *añ*, and *ṇya-* in the sense of offspring; *aṇ*, *ṭhak*, *an*, and *añ* in the sense of dyed with (*rakta*); *aṇ*, *ḍayat*, and *ṅaca* in the sense of desired or fit for (*iṣṭasāma*); *aṇ* in the sense of extracted (*uddhṛta*); *aṇ*, *yat*, and *ṭhak* in the sense of prepared (*saṃskṛta*); *ghan*, *ṭyaṇ*, *yat*, *cha*, and *ṭhañ* in the sense of "belonging to this" (*asya*); *aṇ*, *vuñ*, *yañ*, *ṭhañ*, and *tal* in the sense of a collection denoted by a word ending in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta-samūha*).

The suffix *kha* is used after words denoting sacrifice (*yajña*) in the sense of a collection (*samūha*). In the sense of a collection, there are the suffixes *ṭhak*, *ya*, *ini*, *tra*, and *kyac*. In the sense of play (*krīḍā*), there are *ṇa* and *ñ*. In the sense of Vedic study (*adhyāya*) or the meaning of the Vedas (*vedārtha*), there are *vun* and *ṭhak*. In the sense of "this exists in it" (*asminn asti*), there is *aṇ*; in the sense of "cessation of that" (*tannivṛtti*), there is *aṇ*. In the sense of "dwelling in it" (*nivāsa*), there is *aṇ*; in the sense of "not far from it" (*adūrabhava*), there is *aṇ*. In the senses mentioned above and for the four types of meanings [beginning with "born in"], there are *vuñ*, *chaṇ*, and others. Likewise, *matur* [is added] in the sense of the possessive suffixes (*matup*); *ḍvalac* and *valac* are used in the sense of the possessive suffixes. The suffix *cha* is used in the fourfold sense [of place, origin, etc.]. In the sense of "becoming" (*bhava*), there is *cyap*; in the sense of "fixed" (*dhruva*), there is *cha*. In the sense of contempt (*kutsita*) or proficiency (*prāvīṇya*), there is *vuñ*. In the sense of a place that can be reached (*deśagamya*), there is *cha*.

The suffix *khañ* is used in the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣa*). The suffix *ṭhañ* is used in its own sense (*svārtha*). The suffix *aḥ* is used in the sense of "present time" (*sāmpratika*). The suffix *yañ* is used in the sense of "proximity" (*sāmīpya*). The suffix *ṭhañ* is used in the sense of time (*kāla*), and *ṭhañ* is used in the sense of "originating there" (*bhava*). The suffix *aṇ* is used in the sense of originating from a conjunction of time (*saṃdhivelā*), a season (*ṛtu*), or a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). The suffixes *ṭyu*, *ṭula*, *la*, *ḍimac*, and *ṭayul* are used in the sense of "originating there" (*bhava*). The suffix *dhaḥ*, *aṇ*, and *ṭhap* are used in the sense of "born there" (*jāta*). The suffix *aṇ* is used in the sense of "mostly existing there" (*prāyobhava*), and *aṇ* is used in the sense of "having come into being there" (*samabhūta*). The suffix *ḍhañ* is used in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*). The suffix *ghaḥ* (with the augment *yat*) and *ḍhañ* with the augment *chaḥ* are used in the sense of "originating there" (*bhava*). The suffixes *aṇ*, *ṭhak*, *vuñ*, *ṭhañ*, and *yat* are used in the sense of "coming from that" (*āgata*). The suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of "made of that" (*rūpya*).

The suffix *aṇ* is used in the sense of "originating from that"; *trya* in the sense of "originating from Vidūra"; *aṇ* in the sense of "going to"; *aṇ* in the sense of "departing from"; *aṇ* in the sense of "concerning"; *aṇ* in the sense of "dwelling in"; *aṇ* in the sense of "residing in"; *aṇ* in the sense of "proclaimed by that"; *ṇini* in the sense of "proclaimed"; *ini* in the sense of "studying what was proclaimed"; *aṇ* and other suffixes in the sense of "first known"; *aṇ* and other suffixes in the sense of "belonging to this"; *yat*, *añ*, *ṭhak*, and *vuñ*. The suffix *aṇ* is also used in the sense of "a mark of measurement" and "a hamlet."

Now, regarding the sense of a modification (*vikāra*): there is *aṇ* and so forth; and in the sense of "belonging to this" (*tasyedam*), there is *aṇ*. Furthermore, regarding the sense of a modification, there is *aṇ* and so forth; in the sense of a part (*avayava*), there is *aṇ*; in the sense of a modification, there is *añ*; and also in the sense of a part, there is *añ*. In the sense of a modification such as "attainable" (*prāpya*) and so forth, there is *añ*; in the case of a modification of *śamī*, there is *ṣlañ*; in the sense of a general modification, there is *mayaṭ* and *aṇ*. In the sense of the dung of a cow, there is *mayaṭ*; in the sense of a modification of a female deer (*eṇī*) and so forth, there is *ḍhañ*; in the sense of a modification of a cow, there is *yat*; in the sense of a modification of fruit, there is the suffix *suk*; and in the sense of a modification of *plakṣa* and so forth, there is *aṇ*.

The suffix *ṭhak* is used in the sense of "denying a word"; *ṭhak* in the sense of "calling out"; *ṭhak* and *ṭhaka* in the sense of "inquiring"; *ṭhak* in the sense of "crossing over"; *ṭhak* in the sense of "conquered"; *ṭhak* in the sense of "refined" (*saṃskṛta*); *ṭhak* in the sense of "crossing over"; *ṭhak* in the sense of "conquered"; *ṭhak* in the sense of "won" (*jita*); *ṭhak* in the sense of "refined"; *ṭhak* in the sense of "inquiring"; *ṭhak* and *ṭhan* in the sense of "practicing"; *ṭhak* in the sense of "practicing"; *ṣṭhan* and *ṭhañ* in the sense of "practicing"; *ṭhañ* in the sense of "living"; *ṭhañ* in the sense of "living"; *ṭhak* and *ṣṭhan* in the sense of "carrying away."

The suffix *ṭhak* is used in the sense of "produced" (*nirvṛtta*), "mixed" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*), "doing" (*karoti*), "killing" (*hanti*), and "merchandise" (*paṇya*). The suffix *un* is used in the sense of "merchandise. The suffix *ṭhak* with the augment *ṇa* is used in the sense of "craft" (*śilpa*). The suffix *ṭhak* with the augment *īkak* is used in the sense of "appointed" (*niyukta*). The suffix *ṭhak* is used in the sense of "thought" (*mati*) and "habitual character" (*śīla*). The suffix *ṇa* is used in the sense of "weapon" (*praharaṇa*). The suffix *ṭhak* is used in the sense of "appointed" (*niyukta*). The suffix *ṭhak* is used in the sense of "dwelling" (*vasati*). The suffix *yat* is used in the sense of "piercing" (*vidhyati*). The suffix *yata* is used in the sense of "suitable" (*yogya*), "good" (*sādhu*), and "equal" (*sama*). The suffix *cha* is used in the sense of "purchased" (*krīta*). The suffixes *yat*, *cha*, *thyan*, and *kha* are used in the sense of "beneficial" (*hita*).

The suffix *ṭhañ* is used in the sense of "equal to"; *ṭhak*, *ṭhan*, and *yat* in the sense of "bought"; *kan* in the sense of "worth" (*ārhīya*); *ṭiṭhan* and *ṭhañ* in the sense of "bought"; and *aṇ* in the sense of "belonging to a master" (*īśvara*).

The suffixes *ṭhañ* and others are used in the sense of measure (*parimāṇa*); *ḍa* is used in the sense of a *stoma* or a statement (*vākya*); *ti*, *śāti*, and *ca* are used in the sense of measure; *śat* and *taḥ* are also used in that sense. The suffixes *ṭhañ* and others are used in the sense of "deserving" (*arhati*); specifically, *ṭhañ* and *yac*. The suffix *ṭhañ* is used in the sense of "produced from" (*nirvṛta*). The suffix *vati* is used in the sense of "equal to" (*tulya*) and "like" (*iva*). The suffixes *tva* and *tal* are used in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*); in the sense of abstract state, *imanij*, *iyasun*, and *ṣyañ* are also used. The suffix *ṣyañ* is used in the sense of action (*karman*) as well as abstract state; *ṣyañ* is also used in its own sense (*svārtha*). The suffix *yat* is used in the sense of action and abstract state; *ya*, *ṭhak*, and *yak* are also used in those senses. The suffixes *añ*, *aṇ*, and *vuñ* are used in the sense of action and abstract state. The suffix *khañ* is used in the sense of "breaking the power of the Kṣatriyas" (*kṣatrabhañja*); *ḍhak* and *yat* are also used in that sense.

The suffix *kha* occurs in the sense of attainment; *khañ* occurs in the sense of a name; *kuṇap* occurs in the sense of cooking; *jāhac* occurs in the sense of roots; *cuñcup* occurs in the sense of crossing over; and *śālac* and *śaṅkaṭac* occur in the sense of a specific agent.

The suffix *kaṭac* is used in the sense of a distinguished instrument; *kaṭac* in the sense of dust; *goṣṭhac* in the sense of a place; *kaṭac* in the sense of a collection; *paṭac* in the sense of extension; *goṣṭhac* in the sense of duality; *kaṭac* in the sense of a collection; *paṭac* in the sense of extension; *goṣṭhac* in the sense of duality; *ṣaṅgavac* in the sense of six; *tailac* when expressing oiliness; *kuṭārac* and *kaṭac* in the sense of a distinguished instrument; *ṭīṭac* and *bhraṭac* in the sense of a downward-turned nose; *tyakan* in the sense of proximity and descent; and *aṭhac* in the sense of being engaged in an action.

The suffix *itac* is used in the sense of "having arisen"; *dvayasac* and *mātrac* in the sense of "measure" (*pramāṇa*); *dvayasac* and *dadhnac* in the sense of "vertical measure" (*ūrdhvamāna*). The suffix *aṇ*, *dvayasac*, and *mātrac* are used in the sense of "measurement" (*parimāṇa*). The suffix *vatup* is used in the sense of measurement; specifically, *vatup* is used when the measurement is a number. The suffix *tayap* is used in the sense of a numerical part (*avayava-saṃkhyā*). The suffix *ḍa* is used in the sense of "excess" (*adhika*), and *ḍaṭ* in the sense of "ordinal" (*pūraṇa*). The suffixes *cha*, *yat*, and *tīya* are also used in the sense of ordinal. The suffix *cha* is used in the sense of a well-spoken hymn or a *sāman*; *ghañ* in the sense of what has been studied; *ṭhan* in the sense of what has been eaten; and *ini* in the sense of what has been done.

The suffix *ghan* occurs in the sense of "desired object" (*iṣṭārtha*). The suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* occur in the sense of "that which has been enjoyed" (*bhuktārthaka*). The suffix *ini* occurs in the sense of "accomplished" (*kṛtārtha*).
