The suffix *ini* occurs in the sense of "sought after" (*anveṣaṇārtha*), and also when denoting a name (*saṃjñā*) in the sense of "seen" (*dṛṣṭārtha*). The suffix *matup* occurs in the senses of relation (*sambandha*) and locus (*adhikaraṇa*). The suffix *lac* occurs in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). The suffix *balavadarte lac* occurs in the sense of "acting according to desire" (*kāmavadartha*). The suffixes *ilac*, *śa*, *na*, *ṇa*, *vini*, and *aṇ* occur in the sense of possession. The suffix *urac* occurs in the sense of possession and also in the sense of "height" (*aunnatya*). The suffixes *ra*, *ma*, *va*, *īrat*, *īrac*, and *valac* occur in the sense of possession when a name is implied. The suffixes *ini*, *ṭhan*, *ilac*, and *matup* occur in the sense of possession.

The suffix *ya* is used in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*). The suffixes *vini*, *ārakan*, *ālu*, *inac*, *tap*, *yus*, and *gmini* are used in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). The suffixes *ālac* and *āṭac* are used in the sense of being talkative (*bahubhāṣitatva*). The suffix *sva-āminac* is used in the sense of sovereignty (*aiśvaryārtha*). The suffixes *ac* and *ini* are used in the sense of possession. The suffix *ini* is also used in the sense of possession when the meaning is to be understood through the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*). The suffixes *ba*, *bha*, *yus*, *ti*, *tu*, *ta*, and *yas* are used in the sense of possessing happiness (*sukhimatva*). The suffix *bha-yus* is used in the sense of possession. The suffix *tasil* is used in its own sense (*svārtha*) after words such as *kim* and others; the suffix *tral* is used in its own sense after words ending in the locative case (*saptamī*).

From *idam*, the suffix *ha* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*), while *tasil* is used for time; *hil* with *dā* gives *adhunā*; *hil* with *dā* gives *dānīm*. For "day," *dyas* is used. For the sense of "year," *ut* is used; for "beyond" (*tarārthe*), *āri* is used. For the sense of "day," *edyapi* is used; for "here in this year," *samasaṇ* is used. For the sense of "day," *edyus* is used. For "manner" (*prakāre*), *thāl* and *tham* are used. In the present tense, for its own sense and for the sense of the *astāti* suffixes, *atasuc*, *ril*, *riṣṭātila*, and *āti* are used. For proximity to "not" (*avādhisāmīpye*), *enap* is used; for the sense of *astāti*, *āca* and *āhi* are used. For a word expressing a present number, *dhā* is used in its own sense.

The suffix *pāśap* occurs in the sense of contempt; *tīya* and *ikak* [occur] in the sense of "one of"; *ākanic* occurs in the sense of "alone" (without a companion) or in its own meaning (svārthe); *caraṭ* and *rūpya* occur in the sense of "having been so before" (bhūtapūrva) or in their own meaning; *tamap*, *iṣṭhan*, and *tiṅ* occur in the sense of distinction (*viśiṣṭa*); *tamap* is used when a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) is to be expressed; *ām* occurs in the sense of excellence distinct from the substance (*dravyaprakarṣabhinnārtha*); *tarap* and *īyasun* occur in the sense of expressing a single degree of excellence (*ekātiśayadyotya*); *rūpap* occurs in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*); *tarap* and *īyasun* occur in the sense of incompleteness (*apūrṇa*).

The suffix *rūpa* is used in the sense of praise; *kalpap*, *deśya*, *deśīyar*, *bahuc*, and *akac* are used in the sense of incompleteness; *ka* and *akac* are used in the sense of being unknown; *ka* is used in the sense of contempt; *ra*, *ḍupac*, and *erac* are used in the sense of smallness; *ṣṭarac* is used in the sense of thinness; *ḍatarac* is used for the selection of one out of two; *ḍatamac* is used for the selection of one out of many; *akac* is used in its own sense [of smallness]; *kan*, *ya*, and *cha* are used in the sense of similarity following the word *iva*; *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of abundance; *mayaṭ* is also used in the sense of a locus; *kṛtvasuc* is used in the sense of number in its own sense; *suc* is used in the sense of two or three in its own sense; *suc* is used in its own sense.

The suffix *yat* is used in the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tādarthye*); *trya*, *svārthe* (in the sense of the base itself), *tnap*, *tanap*, *dheya*, *añ*, *tala*, *ka*, *kan*, and *vikan* [are similarly used]. The suffixes *sa* and *sna* are used in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsārthe*). *Aṇ* and *trya* are used in their own sense (*svārthe*). The suffix *śas* is used in the sense of auspiciousness (*maṅgale*) and inauspiciousness (*amaṅgale'rthe*). *Śas* is also used in the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsāyām*). *Tasi* is used in the sense of all case endings (*sārvavibhaktikārthe*). The suffix *cvi* is used in the sense of modification (*vikārārthe*), specifically in the sense of "becoming that which it was not before" (*abhūtatadbhāve*). *Sāti* is used in the sense of totality (*sākalyārthe*), while both *cvi* and *sāti* are used in the sense of pervasion (*vyāptyarthe*).

The suffix *ḍāc* is used after the root *trai* (to protect); *ḍāc* is used in the sense of "stepping out"; *ḍāc* is used in the sense of favorability, opposition, or cooking; *ḍāc* is used in the sense of not swearing or in the sense of shaving; *ḍāc* is used in the sense of auspiciousness or welfare. The prefix *pari* is used in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*). *Upari* and *adhaḥ* are used in the sense of proximity of place or proximity of time. *Sundaraḥ* is used in the sense of uselessness (*vṛthā*). In the sense of excellence: *devaḥ*; in anger: *durvinītaḥ*; in censure: *dhānuṣkaḥ*; in reproach: *cauraḥ*; in affliction: *gataḥ*; in similarity: *paṭuḥ*. (479–480)
Verbal cognition is also twofold: as fragmented (khaṇḍaśaḥ) and as unitary (akhaṇḍaśaḥ). Here, it is called "unitary" because of the synthesis of the fragments. 489

Verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) is twofold: partial verbal comprehension (*khaṇḍaśābdabodha*) and unitary verbal comprehension (*akhaṇḍaśābdabodha*). The first is as follows: in the sentence "Bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), "jar" is the meaning [of the noun], the accusative case-ending has "objectness" (*karmatva*) as its meaning, the root *nī* preceded by the prefix *āṅ* has "bringing" (*ānayana*) as its meaning, and the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) has "effort" (*kṛti*) as its meaning; such is the partial comprehension. The relations (*anvaya*) are the objects of comprehension manifested through syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). Then, the second [type] is the unitary comprehension: "You possess an effort conducive to bringing the jar as the object."

In the Nyāya system, the verbal cognition has the meaning of the nominative case as its primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣya*), as in: "Caitra is the possessor of an effort conducive to the act of bringing the pot. Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*), by the rule that "the verb has the action (*bhāva*) as its primary element," accept a cognition where the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the primary qualificand, such as: "The act of bringing the pot, having Caitra as its agent. Mīmāṃsakas accept a verbal cognition where the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*) is the primary qualificand, as in: "An effort inherent in Caitra, which is conducive to the act of bringing the pot."

Since the first case-ending (*prathamā*) lacks a fixed meaning, its function is to express grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), rather than being enumerated among the *kārakas*. Its expressive power (*śaktatva*) consists in [denoting] agency (*kartṛtva*), singularity (*ekatva*), and non-difference (*abhinnatva*), according to various differing views. The meaning of the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) includes residing-in (*niṣṭhatva*), objecthood (*viṣayatva*), qualificandness (*viśeṣyatva*), modehood (*prakāratva*), counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*), being determined by (*nirūpitatva*), pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*), and so forth.

The meanings of the third case [instrumental] are: agency, instrumentality, being cognized by a cognition, non-difference, concomitance, counter-correlativity, being defined by, residing in, inhering in, simultaneity, and being delimited by.

The meaning of the dative case (caturthī) includes: being the intended object (uddeśyatva), being the cause of satisfaction (tṛptiprayojakatva), being inherent (samavetatva), being the cause of production (niṣpattiprayojakatva), being subject to modification (vikāritva), being the cause of increase (vṛddhiprayojakatva), being dependent (āśritatva), being the object [of cognition] (viṣayatva), being the object of a desire prompted by a desire for one's own removal (svāpaharaṇecchāprayojyecchāviṣayatva), being a prompter (prayojakatva), and being the object of a desire dependent on another desire (icchādhīnecchāviṣayatva), and so forth.

The meaning of the fifth case [the ablative] includes: having a limit (*avadhimattva*), being a counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*), being produced (*janyatva*), dependence on an utterance performed by oneself (*svakartṛkoccāraṇādhīnatva*), being defined (*nirūpitatva*), being made known by cognition (*jñānajñāpyatva*), commencement (*ārambha*), conclusion (*paryanta*), and dependence on a specific word (*tadapadekṣatva*), and so forth.

The meanings of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) include: being an object (*viṣayatva*), being a qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*), being a qualifier (*prakāratva*), ownership (*svatva*), the state of being a signifier (*pratipādakatva*), being uttered (*uccaritatva*), occurrence (*vṛtti*), ownership as defined by [the relation of] lordship (*svāmitā-nirūpitasvatva*), the state of being a signifier, being uttered, counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*), sub-correlativity (*anuyogitva*), non-difference (*abheda*), agency (*kartṛtva*), objecthood (*karmatva*), being a part (*avayavatva*), instrumentality (*karaṇatva*), inherence (*samavetatva*), and the state of being excluded from the referent of a genitive-ending word that lacks the genus which delimits the referent of the word co-uttered with it; such are the various meanings of the genitive. There are many meanings of the genitive.

The meanings of the seventh case (locative) are: the state of being the locus (*ādheyatva*), the state of being an object (*viṣayatva*), the state of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*), the state of being defined (*nirūpitatva*), pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*), non-difference (*abheda*), the state of being delimited (*avacchedyatva*), the state of being a constituent (*ghaṭakatva*), the state of being what is to be expressed (*pratipādyatva*), the state of being a qualifier (*prakāratva*), the relation of co-referentiality (*samānādhikaraṇyātmaka-vaiśiṣṭya*), the state of being what is to be expressed (*pratipādyatva*), the state of being a qualifier (*prakāratva*), the relation of co-referentiality (*samānādhikaraṇyātmaka-vaiśiṣṭya*), contemporaneity (*samānākālikatva*), anteriority (*pūrvakālikatva*), posteriority (*uttarakālikatva*), the state of being the correlate (*anuyogitva*), the state of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*), and dependence upon a desire whose object is oneself (*svaviṣayakecchā'dhīnatva*).

The meanings [of the locative case] are: being excluded from the referents of words ending in the locative suffix that are co-uttered with it and which lack the universal (jāti) that delimits the referent of the word co-uttered with it; and the relation of cause and effect.

The meaning of *iva*, *vā*, *vat*, *yathā*, and so forth is similarity (*sādṛśya*). The meaning of the word *iti* is precisely the meaning of the preceding sentence. The same is the meaning of *ityevamādi* (and so forth) and similar expressions. In the expression "the post is known as a man," the meaning of the word *iti* is "having as its cause a cognition whose qualifier is the delimitor of the referent of the word co-occurring with itself. In the expression "this tree is a *tamāla*," the meaning of the word *iti* is non-difference (*abheda*); thus, it signifies completion (*samāpti*).

The meaning of the word *iti* when uttered in conjunction with a *kim-pada* (an interrogative word) is "having as its cause the desire to know. In the word *iti*, the suffix *ti* signifies the essential form of the word itself. In expressions such as "having seen, he went" (*dṛṣṭvā gataḥ*), the meaning of the constituent elements ending in the suffix *ktvā* is "subsequent time" (i.e., occurring after the action of seeing). For elements ending in the suffix *lyap*, the meaning is likewise "subsequent time. In instances where there is an element ending in the suffix *tumun*, the meaning of that *tumun* suffix is "being prompted by a desire. [Note: The phrase "In instances where there is an element ending in the suffix *tumun*, the meaning of that *tumun* suffix is 'being prompted by a desire'" is repeated in the source text.]

In instances where *tumun* follows a word ending in *tumun*, the meaning of the suffix *tumun* is "being prompted by a desire" (*icchāprayojyatva*), or alternatively, "being an object of a desire dependent upon [another] desire. The meaning of the word *samyak* is "preceded by faith" (*śraddhāpūrvakatva*), as in "he recites correctly" (*samyak paṭhati*). In the case of "he sleeps correctly" (*samyak svapiti*), the meaning of *samyak* is "co-occurrence with the absence of waking cognition" (*jāgraj-jñānābhāva-sāmānādhikaraṇya*). In the case of "it bears fruit correctly" (*samyak phalati*), the meaning is "completeness" (*sampūrṇatva*).

In the expression *samayaṃ namaskaroti* ("he salutes respectfully"), the sense is that it is preceded by devotion (*bhakti*); in *samyak paśyati* ("he sees clearly"), it is preceded by affection (*anurāga*); and in *samyak tāḍayati* ("he strikes properly"), it is preceded by a lack of compassion (*dayā*). These meanings are to be inferred. In *stokaṃ pacati* ("he cooks a little"), the meaning of the word *stoka* is "small. In *sukhaṃ śete* ("he sleeps comfortably"), there is a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward that which produces happiness. In *madhuraṃ rauti* ("he warbles sweetly"), the understanding is: "one who possesses an effort conducive to an activity that is non-different from a sweet warbling."

In the sentence "Caitra alone strikes Maitra," the cognition is that Caitra is the agent of the act of striking whose object is Maitra, and that [the agent] other than Caitra lacks the status of being the agent of the act of striking whose object is Maitra. In the sentence "The lover desires only his beloved," the cognition is that the lover is one who possesses a desire whose object is the beloved, and that he lacks a desire whose object is anyone other than the beloved.

*Āṅ* has the sense of lordship (*īśadarthaka*), pervasion (*abhivyāptārthaka*), boundary (*sīmārthaka*), and that which arises from connection with a verbal root (*dhātuyogajārthaka*). *Ā* also has the sense of recollection (*smaraṇārthaka*) and the sense of a sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). *Aḥ* has the sense of anger and affliction (*kopapīḍārthaka*). *Ku-* has the sense of evil, contempt, and slightness (*pāpakutseṣadarthaka*). *Dhik* has the sense of reproach and censure (*nirbhartsananindārthaka*). *Ca* has the sense of filling a metrical foot (*pādapūraṇa*), collection (*samāhāra*), and conjunction (*samuccaya*). *Svasti* has the sense of benediction, well-being, and merit (*āśīḥkṣemapuṇyārthaka*). *Ati* has the sense of excellence and transgression (*prakarṣollaṅghanārthaka*). *Svit* has the sense of inquiry, deliberation, and reflection (*praśnavitārkārtha*). *Tu* has the sense of distinction and determination (*bhedāvadhāraṇārthaka*). *Sakṛt* has the sense of "only once" (*evārārthaka*).

*Sāra* has the meanings of "far" and "near. *Paścāt* has the meanings of "west," "behind," and "last. *Uta* has the meaning of "option" (*vikalpa*). *Śaśvat* has the meanings of "again" and "together. *Sākṣāt* has the meaning of "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*) and "equal. *Bata* has the meanings of "lamentation," "compassion," "contentment," "wonder," and "addressing. *Hanta* has the meanings of "joy," "compassion," "commencement of speech," and "despair. *Prati* has the meanings of "representative" (*pratinidhi*), "repetition" (*vīpsā*), and "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*). *Iti* has the meanings of "cause" (*hetu*), "context" (*prakaraṇa*), "manifestation" (*prakāśa*), "conclusion" (*samāpti*), and so forth. *Purastāt* has the meanings of "east," "first," "ancient," and "front."

*Yāvat* and *tāvat* signify totality, limit, measure, and restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). *Atho* signifies auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), immediate succession (*anantara*), impossibility (*asambhava*), inquiry (*praśna*), and entirety (*kārtsnya*). *Vṛthā* signifies uselessness (*nirarthaka*) and that which is to be excluded (*varjya*). *Nānā* signifies multiplicity (*aneka*) and both (*ubhaya*). *Nu* signifies inquiry (*pṛcchā*) and option (*vikalpa*). *Anu* signifies posteriority (*paścāt*) and similarity (*sādṛśya*). *Nanu* signifies inquiry (*praśna*), restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), permission (*anujñā*), conciliation (*anunaya*), and address (*āmantraṇa*). *Api* signifies censure (*garhā*), conjunction (*samuccaya*), inquiry (*praśna*), doubt (*śaṅkā*), and possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). *Vā* signifies comparison (*upamā*) and option (*vikalpa*).

*Sāmi* has the sense of partial reproach (*ardha-jugupsā*). *Amā* has the senses of together (*saha*), with (*saha*), and near (*samīpa*). *Evam*, *iva*, and *ittham* have the senses of manner (*prakāra*), comparison (*upamā*), acceptance (*aṅgīkāra*), and restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). *Nūnam* has the senses of conjecture (*tarka*) and certainty (*niścaya*). *Kim* has the senses of inquiry (*pracchā*) and reproach (*jugupsana*). *Nāma* has the senses of manifestation (*prākāśya*), possibility (*saṃbhāvya*), anger (*krodha*), approach (*upagama*), and censure (*kutsana*). *Alam* expresses the senses of ornament (*bhūṣaṇa*), sufficiency (*paryāpti*), capability (*śakti*), and prohibition (*vāraṇa*). *Huṃ* has the senses of deliberation (*vitarka*) and inquiry (*paripraśna*). *Samayā* has the senses of proximity (*antika*) and middle (*madhya*).

Furthermore: *apra-* signifies non-existence and non-difference; *niḥ* signifies certainty and negation; *kila* signifies report and possibility; *purā* signifies proximity to a sequence, the near future, and the distant past; *ūrī*, *urī*, and *urarī* signify expansion and acceptance; *khalu* signifies negation, embellishment of a sentence, inquiry, and conciliation; *abhitaḥ* signifies proximity, both sides, speed, totality, and facing toward.

*Prāduḥ* signifies manifestation or appearance; *mithaḥ* signifies mutual secrecy or privacy; *tiraḥ* signifies disappearance or transversality; *hā* signifies dejection, grief, distress, or reproach; *ahaha* signifies wonder or affliction; *hi* signifies cause or emphasis; *ciraṃ*, *cirāya*, *cirarātrāya*, *cirasya*, *acireṇa*, *cirāt*, *cire*, and *ciram* signify length of time; *muhuḥ*, *punaḥ-punaḥ*, *śaśvat*, *abhīkṣṇaṃ*, and *asakṛt* signify repetition or frequency.

*tatkṣaṇam*, *strāk*, *bhaktaṭi*, *tityañjasā*, *ahāya*, *drāṅ*, *maṃkṣu*, and *sapadi* have the meaning of "instantly" or "quickly. *Druta* has the same meaning. *Atiśaya* signifies "excess" or "intensity"; *balavat*, *suṣṭhu*, *kimuta*, *svasti*, and *atīva* signify "exceedingly" or "intensely. *Varjanam*, *pṛthak*, *vinā*, *antareṇa*, *ṛte*, and *hiruk* have the meaning of "separation," "without," or "except. *Hetuḥ*, *yataḥ*, *tat*, *tataḥ*, and *yataḥ* have the meaning of "because" or "since. *Cit* and *cana* signify "incomplete" or "not at all. *Jātu* and *kadācit* have the meaning of "perhaps" or "at some time. *Saha*, *sārdham*, *sākam*, *satrā*, *samam*, and *sahā* have the meaning of "together with. *Prādhvam* has the meaning of "favorably" or "conformably."

*mudhā*, *vyarthaka*, *vṛthā*, and *arthaka* signify "in vain" or "uselessly. *Virtaka*, *aho*, *āho*, *utāho*, *kim*, and *kimuta* have meanings such as "oh" or "indeed. *Tu*, *hi*, *ca*, *sma*, *ha*, and *vai* are used for the purpose of filling the meter (*pādapūraṇa*). *Su*, *suṣṭhu*, *cāru*, *pūjana*, *bhṛśa*, *smṛddhi*, and so forth, signify "excellent," "beautiful," "praise," "intense," "prosperity," and the like. *Agram*, *puraḥ*, and *purataḥ* signify "the front" or "ahead. *Amutra* and *pretya* signify "in another state of existence" (after death). *Va*, *vā*, *yathā*, *tathā*, *eva*, and *evam* signify "equality" or "likewise. *Aho* and *hī* signify "wonder. *Tūṣṇīm* and *tūṣṇīkām* signify "silence" or "mauna."

*Divya* has the sense of "heavenly" (*śam*). *Upajoṣam* has the sense of "enjoying. Words having the sense of "auspicious" (*kalyāṇa*) or "purpose" (*artha*) [occur here]. *Antarā*, *antareṇa*, and *antare* have the sense of "in the middle" (*madhya*). *Prasahya* has the sense of "forcefully" (*haṭha*). *Ucitam*, *sāmpratam*, and *sthāne* have the sense of "proper" (*yukta*). *Abhīkṣṇam*, *śaśvat*, *anāratam*, and *nirantaram* have the sense of "continually" (*anārata*). *A*, *ana*, *nahi*, *no*, and *na* have the sense of "not even a little" (*svalpa*), as well as negation (*pratiṣedha*) and absence (*abhāva*). *Mā sma* and *mā alam* are used for prohibition (*vāraṇa*). *Cet* and *yadi* have the sense of "an alternative view" (*pakṣāntara*). *Uddhā* and *añjasā* have the sense of "truth" (*tattva*). *Prāduḥ* and *āviḥ* have the sense of "manifest" (*prakaṭa*).

*Oṃ* is used for salutation. *Evaṃ* has the sense of "so" or "thus. *Paramam* has the sense of "exceedingly. *Anumati* has the sense of "consent. *Paritaḥ*, *sarvataḥ*, *viśvak*, and *samantāt* have the sense of "on all sides" or "everywhere. *Astu* has the sense of "granting permission. *Nanu* and *ca* have the sense of "contradiction" or "objection. *Kaccit* has the sense of "inquiry regarding what is desired. *Niḥṣamam* and *duḥṣamam* have the sense of "blame" or "censure. *Yathāsvam* and *yathāyatham* have the sense of "appropriate manner" or "as is fitting. *Mṛṣā* and *mithyā* have the sense of "untruth" or "falsity. *Yāvat* has the sense of "extent" or "as much as. *Evam*, *tu*, *punaḥ*, *vai*, *eva*, *hi*, and *ava* have the sense of "determination" or "emphasis. *Nūnam* and *avaśyam* have the sense of "certainty" or "necessity."

*Arvāk* has the sense of "below" or "hitherward. *Ām* and *evam* have the sense of certainty or affirmation. *Svayam*, *ātmanā*, and *nijam* have the sense of "by oneself" or "inherently. *Nīcaiḥ* has the sense of "little" or "low. *Uccaiḥ* has the sense of "great" or "high. *Prāyaḥ* and *bahulam* have the sense of "mostly" or "frequently. *Śanaiḥ* has the sense of "slowly" or "gradually. *Sanāt* and *sanat* have the sense of "eternal" or "perpetually. *Sma* has the sense of the past tense. *Astam* has the sense of "disappearance" or "setting. *U* has the sense of "anger" or "harsh speech. *Ūm* has the sense of a question. *Ayī* has the sense of conciliation or soothing. *Huṃ* has the sense of deliberation or reflection. *Duṣṭhu* has the sense of censure or reproach.

*Suṣṭhu* has the sense of "well" or "praise. *Prage* has the sense of "at dawn" or "in the morning. *Nikaṣā* has the sense of "nearby. *Parut* has the sense of "last year. *Parāri* and *aiṣamaḥ* have the senses of "the year before last" and "this year," respectively. *Paredyavi* has the sense of "on the following day. *Hyas* has the sense of "yesterday. *Paraśvas* has the sense of "the day after tomorrow. *Etarhi*, *samprati*, *idānīm*, *adhunā*, and *sāmpratam* have the sense of "now" or "at this time. *Caṭacaṭādiḥ*, *humphaṭ*, *hu*, and *vāidistomaḥ* [are onomatopoeic or exclamatory sounds].

*Huṃ* is the seed-syllable of anger (*krodhabīja*); *phaṭ* is the seed-syllable of the weapon (*astrabīja*). *Hāvu*, *hāvu*, and *bāvu* are portions of mantras (*stomāḥ*) that possess modern conventions. The particles beginning with *ca* (*cādayaḥ nipātāḥ*) are used in their own sense, as well as for conjunction and so forth. The particles beginning with *pra* (*prādayaḥ*) signify excellence and other such meanings. *Temanaṃ* signifies a side-dish (*vyañjana*). *Gauḥ* is conventional (*rūḍha*). *Gaṅgā* indicates the bank by secondary indication (*tīralakṣaka*). *Paṅkajaṃ* is both etymological and conventional (*yogarūḍha*). *Pācakaṃ* is purely etymological (*yaugika*). *Maṇḍapaḥ* is both etymological and conventional (*yaugikarūḍhā*). *Mahārajataṃ* denotes gold. *Ahaṃ* expresses the power of the agent (*kartṛśaktikatam*).

Established denotation (*ruḍhasaṃjñā*) is of four kinds: based on a cause (*naimittikī*), conventional (*pāribhāṣikī*), and conditional (*aupādhikī*). Among these, that which possesses a convention delimited by a genus (*jāti*) is "based on a cause," as in the case of *go* (cow) or *Caitra*. That which is established by convention is "conventional," such as "ether" (*ākāśa*) as that which has sound as its substratum, or "beast" (*paśu*) as that which possesses a tail; by convention, a wooden elephant is called a *hittha*, a wealthy man is called a *śreṣṭhin*. That which is [determined] by a condition (*upādhi*) or by action is "conditional," such as "fickle" (*capala*) or "unsteady" (*cañcala*) due to the quality of instability; "elements" (*bhūtāni*) such as earth; "insentient" (*jaḍa*) as a living being devoid of movement; and "fool" (*mūrkha*) as a living being devoid of learning and the like.

A "mute" (mūka) is a living being devoid of speech. According to modern terminology, "subjectness" (pakṣatā) and so forth are technical definitions; "prakṛti" is threefold, namely nouns such as *ghaṭa* (pot) and others. Verbs (*dhātu*) such as *bhū*, *as*, and *kṛñ* possess the power of action. Nominal stems (*prātipadika*) include words like *rāma* and others; there are also figurative ones, such as *dākṣi-pācaka*. Universal classes (*jāti*) and partless adjuncts (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) appear by their own nature. "Valid cognition" (*pramā*) and "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) function as technical definitions for that which conveys meaning. The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) generate verbal comprehension. The suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* signify excellence (*prakarṣa*).

The possessive suffix *matup* conveys meanings such as praise (*praśaṃsā*). In the word *bhavatī*, it is the factor that delimits the capacity to generate verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) and fulfills the requirement of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). Some maintain, however, that prefixes such as *pra-* and *parā-* serve to establish the conventional status (*nirūḍhatva*) of a word even when it functions through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*). All nominal suffixes (*sup*), verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), primary derivatives (*kṛt*), and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) are *svārtha* (expressing their own meaning); by the force of grammatical connection (*yoga*), they may also refer to number and other properties. Derivatives such as the desiderative (*san*) and the intensive (*tal*) express only the root's own form (*svarūpamātra*). Furthermore, primary nominal suffixes (*ghañ*) prescribed to denote the abstract action (*bhāva*) also express only the root's own form.

Based on grammatical rules (*anuśāsana*), adverbs are accepted as having the properties of singularity, being objects of action (*karman*), and being neuter. When qualifying the meaning of an affix (*pratyayārtha*), they appear in the nominative case; however, when qualifying the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*), they convey the meanings of singularity, objecthood, and the neuter gender. The verb form *sthīyate* (it is stayed) conveys the present tense, *gataṃ* (gone) conveys the past, and *draṣṭavyaṃ* (to be seen) conveys the future, respectively. "Drinking" (*pānam*) is the operation conducive to the contact of a liquid substance with a location below the throat.

*Āvāpa* is inclusion; *udvāpa* is exclusion. *Prāpti* and *parihāra* denote attainment and avoidance. *Vivaraṇa* is the state of having an identical meaning. A *kakuda* is one who bestows a daughter with ornaments and honors. *Svārājya* is the status of Indra. *Svaḥ* is a word indicating eternal bliss and heaven. *Lakṣaṇā* is a function [of a word] that exists when there is a connection with the primary meaning; that which possesses this is *lakṣaka*. In the phrase "the collection goes," it means "the people in the collection go. The word *saundhava* has the power (*śakti*) to denote both salt and a horse. Words such as *gāc* and *māc* are modern conventions (*saṃketita*).

The Mīmāṃsakas consider even a sentence to be indicative (*lakṣaka*), as in "the owner of brindled cows" (*citragosvāmī*). In "the Vāhīka is an ox" (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*), there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to one who resembles an ox. The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). The Alaṃkārikas accept indication within a sentence; for instance, in the root *kas*, there is indication in the sense of "blossomed. The word *dhenuḥ* (cow) is a conventional term (*rūḍhi*) by its primary power (*śakti*) denoting a cow distinguished by the act of milking. There is primary power (*śakti*) in single syllables, such as *na* [meaning "not"] or *kha* [meaning "sky"]; however, in a composite whole, it is *nakha* [meaning "nail"]. A word is both etymological and conventional (*yogarūḍha*) in the case of *tailam* (oil): by etymology (*yoga*) it means "produced from sesame," but by convention (*rūḍhi*) it means "ointment."

By virtue of both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), the words "oil" (*taila*) and "leaf" (*patra*) [denote a lotus]. By derivation, *paṅkaja* means a water-lily (*kumuda*); by convention, it means a lotus (*padma*). In the case of compounds based on both derivation and convention, examples include *kṛṣṇasarpa* ("black snake") and *lohitaśalya* ("red-tipped arrow"). Even words ending in *kṛt* suffixes that are derived-conventional, such as *paṅkaja*, possess the nature of being compound-based. The suffix *ikaṇ* is used in its own sense (without changing the meaning). *Padmanābha*, *Yudhiṣṭhira*, and *Manasādevī* are examples of words that are both derivative and conventional. Derivative words (*yaugika*) are threefold: compound, formed with secondary (*taddhita*) suffixes, and ending in *kṛt* suffixes. Even a copulative compound (*dvandva*) can be derivative. *Brāhmaṇī*, *śvaśrū*, and *śūdrā* are derivative; [the feminine suffixes] *ṅīp*, *āṅ*, and *āp* [are also derivative].

The term *brāhmaṇī* denotes a Brāhmaṇa qualified by femininity. Compounds possess a collective power (*samudāya-śakti*), where "collectivity" (*samudāyatva*) is the state of being the object of a specific relative cognition (*apekṣā-buddhi*). A word (*pada*) is that which ends in an inflectional suffix (*vibhakti*), or alternatively, a word is a meaningful unit ending in either a nominal suffix (*sup*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). A sentence (*vākya*) is either a collection of words ending in *sup* and *tiṅ*, or a group of words possessing mutual semantic expectancy (*samartha*). Furthermore, a word is also a suggester (*vyañjaka*); and through the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā-vṛtti*), there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the root of which indication is the power of suggestion (*vyañjanā-śakti*).

Denotation (*abhidhā*) is the power of a word; it too is the root of suggestion (*vyañjanā*), and thus the root is the cooperative cause. The function [of denotation] that abandons its own primary meaning (*jahatsvārthā*) occurs, for example, in the case of the word "Ganges" when applied to its bank. The function that does not abandon its own primary meaning (*ajahatsvārthā*) pertains to both the denoted and the indicated meanings, as in the case of the word "jar" when applied to a substance, or the word "blue jar" when applied to a substance. Established indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) possesses beginningless intentionality, as in the cases of *aruṇam* (red) and *aruṇayā gavā somam krīṇāti* (one buys Soma with a red cow). Modern indication (*ādhunikī lakṣaṇā*) possesses a beginning intentionality, as in the case of the word "jar" in its capacity as a jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*).

The secondary (gauṇī) function is seen in the case of "The boy is fire" (*agnir māṇavakaḥ*), meaning "the boy is similar to fire. The knowledge of the word—whether by way of its primary power (*śakti*) or its indicative power (*lakṣaṇā*)—is the cause [of comprehension]. Through the primary function (*abhidhā*), there is cognition by the mind aided by memory; through the indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*), there is also cognition by the mind aided by memory; and through the suggestive function (*vyañjanā*), there is likewise the cognition of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*). Or rather, there is the cognition of the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) by the mind aided by memory.

Even for the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*), there is a distinctness [of function] from denotation (*abhidhā*), indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and suggestion (*vyañjanā*), because these operate in conjunction with memory (*smṛti*). A *vṛtti* (function) is a convention (*saṃketa*) that regulates the presentation of word-meanings; since the knowledge of intention (*tātparya*) is directly useful for verbal comprehension, intention itself is not of the nature of a *vṛtti*. However, it is necessary for indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to possess the status of a *vṛtti*. The relationship between the two word-meanings—the signified and the signifier—is an independent relation.

The Mīmāṃsakas, who maintain the eternity of words (*padanityatvavādinaḥ*), hold that the expressive power of words consists in their capacity to denote meanings based on the potentiality inherent in the knowledge of those meanings. Kumārila Bhaṭṭa, however, accepts that the relation between word-meanings (*padārthasaṃsarga*) is also denotable. The cognition of this potentiality (*śaktijñāna*) is of two kinds—comprehending the denotative capacity of the word toward its meaning, and comprehending the denotability of the word in respect to the meaning—and both serve as the cause for verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). Expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is the regulator of the manifestation of the relation; the relation between two word-meanings is obtained through the force of expectancy.

The status of being a *pravṛttinimitta* (the ground for the application of a word) consists in being denotable, while being resident in that which is denoted, and being a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the presentation of that which is denoted. Regarding the principle that "a word-meaning (*padārtha*) connects with a word-meaning, but not with a part of a word-meaning," the status of being a word-meaning (*padārthatva*) therein consists in being the object of a convention by virtue of being the substratum of the objective content of a cognition; whereas the status of being a part thereof (*tadekadeśatva*) consists in being the object of a convention by virtue of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the objective content of a cognition—that very thing is the *śakyatāvacchedaka* (the delimitor of the denotability).

The word *ākāśa* (ether) has its primary denotative power (*śakti*) in that which is unconditioned. Alternatively, one may accept that the word *ākāśa* possesses secondary denotative power (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of being a substance distinct from the eight [material] substances, or in the sense of being the denotation of the word *ākāśa*. Or else, there is a primary verbal cognition in the form "ether is the substratum of sound. However, in cases such as "there is no substance" or "there is no cow," secondary denotation applies; thus, [terms like] "heavenly cow" (*svargadhenū*) and the like are metaphorical. The Prābhākaras, however, maintain that the word *dhenū* (cow) has its primary denotative power in that which is qualified by the state of being the object of milking (*dhānakarmatā*), and not in that which is qualified by cowness (*gotva*).

Regarding the apprehension of the word *puṣpavanta* as denoting both the sun and the moon, because the objective referents residing in both are one and the same, there arises the cognition that the property of being the moon and the property of being the sun—both of which have the status of being the delimitors of the property of the subject (*dharmitāvacchedakatā*) in a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*)—are fully present as the delimiters of the denotative power (*śakyatāvacchedakatva-paryāpti*). Thus, the convention (*saṃketa*) regarding the word *puṣpavanta* is: "May there arise from the word *puṣpavanta* a verbal cognition whose object is delimited by the property of being the moon and whose object is delimited by the property of being the sun."

Because the denotative function (*śakti*) is one—due to the unity of the objective reference residing in the cognition, which is delimited by the state of having both as its object—there is no polysemy. Even the *Amarakośa*, with the single expression "the sun and the moon," [demonstrates this] through that single power. Furthermore, because the power of pronouns is also one, they do not possess polysemy. As for words such as "Hari" and the like, their power resides in multiple meanings. Regarding the pronouns *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the divine will constitutes the convention: "Let there be a cognition qualified by the word 'you' (or 'I')."

In the first case, the relation of qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is by way of two relations: (1) having as its object a property delimited by the condition of being the delimiting factor of the objective referent (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) of a desire whose qualifier is the state of being the substratum of the cognition produced by a sentence composed of itself; and (2) being produced by itself. In the second case, the relation of qualification is by way of two relations: (1) having as its object a property delimited by the condition of being the delimiting factor of the status of being the utterer (*uccārayitṛtva*) of itself; and (2) being produced by itself.

Since "ownership" (svatva) is included within the scope of the relation [of verbal suffixes], there is no lack of uniformity (ananugama). In the case of the statement, "He said, 'I am this learned man, I know [this],' " the sentence-meaning is not the object (karman) in all instances; rather, the word *iti* refers to that which has the same form as the cognition produced by that sentence. The meaning of *iti* is a qualifier, through non-difference, of both the root-meaning and the cognition that delimits it. Thus, in every instance, including cases involving subordinate sentences containing the word *yuṣmat* ("you"), the word *iti* refers to that which has the same form as the cognition produced by that specific sentence.

In such cases as "You are fat" and "I am fat," or "You will enjoy heaven" and "I will enjoy heaven," because the primary referents of the words *yuṣmad* (you) and *asmad* (I) are indeed the bodies and the selves of the person being addressed and the speaker respectively, the meanings of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are restricted to those two alone. In the statement "All pots possess color," the meaning of the word *sarva* (all) is the state of being without exception.

The basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word "all" (*sarva*) is a property that is co-extensive with the predicate (*vidheya*) and pervades the delimitor of the subjecthood (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*). In this context, such a property is the "totality" (*yāvattva*) residing in jars and other objects; it pervades "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), which is a collective property (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), and is pervaded by color and other qualities. The relationship of pervasion and being pervaded is understood through implication. Furthermore, the state of pervading the delimitor of subjecthood consists in not being a delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of a mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) that is co-located with it. Moreover, the "totality" (*yāvattva*) is not distinct from its own inherence (*paryāpti*).

The state of being pervaded by the predicate (vidheya-vyāpyatva), however, consists in the possession of the absence of that specific predicate, which has as its counter-correlate (pratiyogitā) that which is delimited by the respective delimitor of the predicatehood (vidheyatāvacchedaka) and whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of deviation (vyabhicāritva). In the case of the sentence "All things are existent at time," the meaning of the word "all" (sarva), which is co-referential with the word expressing the predicate, is "as-many-ness" (yāvattva) whose pervasion is determined by a relation delimited by the delimitor of the subjecthood (uddeśyatāvacchedaka) which is itself pervasive of the delimitor of the predicatehood, and which possesses a collective inherence (paryāpti).

Regarding the statement "Time possesses all properties" (*kālaḥ sarvadharmavān*), here too, by the word "all" (*sarva*), what is intended as the object of cognition is a totality (*yāvattva*) that is pervaded by the relation to time and so forth—which are the pervaders of possession of occurrence—and which is co-extensive with [those properties]. In the statement "All is knowable" (*sarvaṃ prameyam*), the word "all" has the meaning of a totality that is co-extensive with the predicate, which is not delimited by the counter-correlativity of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāvapratiyogitānavacchedaka*).

In the sentence "This person knows every pot," since it is an empirical fact that the objecthood expressed by the second case suffix (dvitīyārtha-viṣayatā) is construed as the relatum (nirūpakatayā) within the cognition of this person, the denotative power (śakti) of the word *sarva* resides in that which is delimited by a universal number (*yāvattva*) which is the counter-correlate of a pervasion (*paryāpti*)—wherein potness (*ghaṭatva*) is the pervader and the objecthood of the cognition of this person is the pervaded.

In this context, regarding the statement "not all forms" (*na sarvāṇi rūpāṇi*), the word *sarva*—which functions as a qualifier of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the negative particle (*nañ*)—denotes a totality (*yāvatva*) that is the locus of a pervasion (*vyāpaka-paryāpti-nirūpaka*) over its own referent’s property of being a form (*rūpatva*) and so forth. Consequently, the absence delimited by that [totality] is indeed uncontradicted in the case of a jar and other such things. In the cognition "all substance is not possessed of form" (*sarvaṃ dravyaṃ na rūpavat*), there is understood an absence of co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya-bhāva*) with the totality that pervades substanceness (*dravyatva*). Thus, the negative particle conveys the absence precisely as delimited by the qualifier of the locus (*anuyogi-viśeṣaṇa*).

In the sentence, "Caitra has eaten curd, Maitra milk, Jaitra ghee, but Paitra has eaten everything," the word *sarva* possesses a distinct power (*śakti*) consisting of a convention (*saṃketa*) that generates a cognition having as its qualifier all such properties [as those previously mentioned]. However, in the case of the statement, "The New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) are performed for one who desires any other specific rewards," there is the attainment through conjunction (*yogasiddhi*), because each person desiring an individual result has the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to them; thus, through the conjunction of each individual performance, the respective results are produced.

By the phrase "in sequence" (*krameṇa*), the position that [the word] *sarvebhyaḥ* (to all) is used in its distributive application as *pratyekasmai* (to each one) is strengthened. The word *kim* has the power [to denote] that which is desired to be known; the property (*dharma*) intended by the speaker is the basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*). However, in the case of "Whose son is handsome? (*kasya putraḥ sundaraḥ*), there is understood a desire whose object is the knowledge of the predicate currently under discussion, where the delimiting factor of the objective reference (*uddeśyatāvacchedakatā*) is delimited by that very [property] as qualified by a specific property.

When there is an inquiry regarding a particular property delimited by a specific attribute—as in the question "Who is this?"—the power [of the pronoun] resides in the aspect delimited by "this-ness" (idantva); the resulting cognition is that the person possesses the property sought after as the delimiting factor of the predicate (vidheyatāvacchedaka).

In the cases of "What substance is this?", "Whose wealth is this?", "Is this the work of your son?", and "Whose son are you?", the cognition is as follows: "This is non-different from a substance which is non-different from that which possesses a specific property of substanceness (dravyatva) which is sought after as the delimiting factor of the delimitorship [of the predicate], which is delimited by the predicate-property itself, which is related through identity, and which is the delimitorship of the predication delimited by the subjecthood delimited by 'this-ness'. In other words, the understanding is: "This is a substance identical with that which possesses a specific attribute of being a substance."

Regarding the question "Whose is this?", the denotative power (*śakti*) of the word *kim* resides in that which is delimited by a property that is co-extensive with, yet subordinate to, the relation of being the counter-correlative of the desire to know (*jijñāsita-nirūpitatva*), where this desire is characterized by being the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) determined by a relation of being the qualificandum (*vidheyatā-nirūpita-nirūpitatva-sambandha-avacchinna-avacchedakatva*). This qualificandumness is, in turn, determined by a subject (*uddeśyatā*) that is delimited by a property presented by a word co-uttered with [the word *kim*] itself (*sva-samabhivyāhṛta-pada-upasthāpyatā-avacchedaka-dharma-avacchinna-uddeśyatā-nirūpita*). Furthermore, it is delimited by a property that serves as the delimitor of the connection of its own meaning (*svārtha-anvayatā-avacchedaka-dharma-avacchinna-vidheyatā-nirūpita-nirūpitatva-sambandha-avacchinna-avacchedakatva*). Thus, the power of *kim* pertains to that which is delimited by a property that is not wider than the counter-correlativity of the desire to know.

The cognition is: "This [object] possesses ownership (svatva) characterized by a property lower than that which is the counter-correlate of the relation of being sought to be known as the delimitor of the delimitor of the predication-ness (vidheyatā) delimited by ownership-ness (svatvatva) as determined by this [object]. In that context, the usage of the subsequent sentence is "this is one's own" (svīyam). In the case of "How many are your sons?", the meaning of the interrogative pronoun *kiṃ* is construed non-differently with the number that is the delimitor of the predication-ness.

Regarding the question "Whose son are you?", the word *kiṃ* (what) is construed non-differently with the sense of "being produced" (*janyatva*), which serves as the delimitor of the scope of the predicate (*vidheyatāvacchedaka*) in the genitive case-meaning. In the first case, the denotative power (*śakti*) of the word *kiṃ* is delimited by a property that occurs in a narrower domain than the property characterized by being the delimitor of the scope of non-differential co-referentiality (*abhedānvayitāvacchedakatva*) with the object of inquiry (*jijñāsita-svārtha*). In the second case, the denotative power is delimited by a property that occurs in a narrower domain than the property characterized by being the delimitor of the scope of non-differential co-referentiality with the object of inquiry.

In the expression "Is it the moon? Is it a lotus?", there is a cognition consisting of the speaker's conjecture regarding the meaning of the indeclinable *kimaḥ* used in the sense of deliberation (*vitarka*). This is a conjecture whose qualifier is the moon and so forth, occurring non-differently. The moon is construed with that [conjecture] through the relation of being a qualifier (*prakāritā*), while the cognition itself is construed with the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*)—which is presented by the word ending in the nominative case—through the relation of being the qualificandum-ness (*viśeṣyatā*).

"Apprehension" (*saṃbhāvanā*) means doubt; this [term] is to be supplied [in the context]. Thus, there arises a cognition whose qualificandum is the moon, related to a qualifier delimited by the relation of non-difference and connection, and which has as its qualificandum-ness that delimited by "this-ness" (*idantva*), through the relation of qualificandum-ness (*viśeṣyatā*). According to the school of Poetics (*ālaṃkārika*), the verbal comprehension here results from suggestion (*vyañjanā*); according to the school of Logicians (*naiyāyika*), it is a mental cognition.

In expressions such as "Who other than you does not give? (*tvadanyaḥ ko na dadāti*), the denotative power (*śakti*) of the interrogative pronoun *kim* resides in that which is delimited by a property whose pervasion (*paryāpti*) is not a delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*). [The meaning is: "You alone are distinct from the agent of giving" (*tvameva dānakartṛbhinnaḥ*); "everyone other than you is an agent of giving" (*tvadanyaḥ sarvo dānakartā*). The negative particle (*nañ*) serves to indicate the speaker's intention (*tātparya*). The word *kim* possesses multiple denotative powers (*nānārthaśaktayaḥ*). In the expression "Who knows this? (*idaṃ ko jānīte*), the cognition is: "one who lacks the state of being a locus of knowledge having this as its object" (*idaṃviṣayakajñānāśrayatvābhāvavān*). When used in the sense of censure, the word *kim* is as in "What a cow! (*kiṃ gaur iti*).

The word *yat* has its denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to that which is delimited by a property characterized by being the objective of the speaker’s cognition as the object to be conveyed by the word *tat*. The word *yat*, when referring back to what has been previously introduced (*prakrānta*), has its denotative power with respect to that which is delimited by a property residing in the cognition [of the hearer] as the delimitor of the state of being presented by the word preceding it, uttered by the person uttering it. The word *tat* has its denotative power with respect to the object presented by the word *yat*. The word *tad* has its denotative power with respect to the object presented by a word previously employed. Thus, although the word *tat* possesses denotative power toward a well-known object, [it functions here as a pronoun referring back to a specific antecedent].

The word *idam* has denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to an object that is the focus of direct perception; the word *etad* likewise. The word *adas* has denotative power with respect to an object that is the focus of indirect (non-perceptual) cognition. The word *sva* (self) has denotative power with respect to that which is presented by a word co-occurring with it. Co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) consists in being a constituent part of the same word. The word *sva* has denotative power with respect to both: that which is the qualificand of its own meaning—either directly or through a series—and that which is the referent of a word expressing an action or a kāraka (participant in an action) co-occurring with it.

In cases such as "Caitra sees" (*caitraḥ paśyati*), "is seen by his own son Caitra" (*svaputracaitreṇa dṛśyate*), "Caitra sees himself" (*caitraḥ svam paśyati*), "Maitra sees his own son who was looked at by Caitra" (*caitreṇāvalokitaṃ svaputraṃ maitraḥ paśyati*), and "the mountain possesses smoke which pervades its own [locus] and is pervaded by fire," the cognition is established according to the circumstances through either primary denotation (*śakti*) or secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Even in instances such as "He sees his own son" (*brahmaṇaḥ svaputraṃ paśyati*) and "One should approach one's wife during the fertile period" (*ṛtau bhāryām upeyāt*), the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) occurs through a dual relation: having oneself as the locus (*svāśrayatva*) and being the progenitor of a son who is the object of the seeing that has oneself as its determiner (*svanirūpakadarśanaviṣayaputrajanakatva*).

There is a denotative power (śakti) with respect to that which is delimited by a property characterized by being present in the speaker’s cognition—whether directly or indirectly—as the delimitor of the objectness (viśeṣyatā) determined by an objectness residing in one's own purpose; likewise, there is a denotative power with respect to that which is delimited by a property characterized by being present in the speaker’s cognition as the delimitor of the state of being construed with a verb co-occurring with itself through the mediation of the meaning of an inflection (vibhakti). Thus, when the intended meaning (tātparya) is present in each case, comprehension proceeds without obstruction.

The word *eka* has its denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to that which is qualified by isolation (*kaivalya*) and so forth. Isolation (*kaivalya*) is the state of being devoid of a second of the same class (*sajātīya*), which is the non-counterpositiveness of a difference residing in what is of the same class. Being devoid of a second of the same class is the non-counterpositiveness of a difference residing in what is of the same class. Being of the same class (*sajātīyatva*) is the possession of the property to be predicated (*vidheya*) in the context at hand. In the sentence "This one person eats here" (*ayam eko bhukte*), the cognition produced is: "This person eats here, being the non-counterpositive of a difference residing in the agent of eating whose locus is this particular place."

The convention (*saṃketa*) is: "Let there be a cognition qualified by both [of the following] relations: (1) being produced by itself, and (2) having as its object that which is not the counter-correlative (*apratiyogin*) of a difference residing in what is always non-existent with respect to itself. However, in the case of the expression "cows consisting of bodies" (*piṇḍamayyo gāvaḥ*), the understanding occurs through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that power (*śakti*) is "crooked" (*kubjā*) with respect to the individual (*vyakti*) portion; yet this crookedness does not serve as the basis for the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of denotability (*vācyatva*). Alternatively, power is simply a distinct category of entity (*padārthāntara*).

Maṇḍanamiśra, however, holds that indication (lakṣaṇā) conveys the individual through the mode of the genus; there is also another position that the expressive power (śakti) resides in the form (ākṛti) and indication in the individual. The Prābhākaras, on the other hand, maintain that the recollection of the individual arises from a mental impression (saṃskāra). They also postulate auxiliary cognition based on both the nature of being a power and the nature of being a relation. Alternatively, the cause of verbal comprehension is a cognition whose qualifier is the word and whose relation is the function (vṛtti). Or rather, the expressive power of words such as "cow" resides precisely in the cognition of cowness and so forth, where the relation is inherence (samavāya) and the like. || 481 ||
Dharma and adharma, known as the "unseen force" (apūrva), consist of the propitiation of Hari;
they are considered to be either two mats or two persons, according to different systems of thought. (482)

In the Nyāya system, *dharma* has the sense of merit (*puṇya*), while *dharma* and *adharma* have the sense of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*). In Mīmāṃsā, *dharma* is the unseen merit (*apūrva*); in Upāsanā, *dharma* is the propitiation of the Lord. The word *dharma* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) for an object characterized by an injunction (*codanā-lakṣaṇa*). In the statement "The Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo'dhyetavyaḥ*), the suffix *-tavya* signifies verbal productive energy (*śābdabhāvanā*). *Dharma* is the knowledge of the meaning of the Veda. The term "desire to know" (*jijñāsā*) indicates, through the function of exclusive indication (*jahallakṣaṇā*), an inquiry accomplished by desire.

The meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is the relationship between the goal and the means (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*). In the word *jijñāsā*, "knowledge" (*jñāna*)—specifically that which possesses causal power—is intended, by way of non-abandoning indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*), to mean knowledge conducive to practice. The resulting cognition is: "An inquiry, which is to be accomplished by the desire for knowledge conducive to practice, must be undertaken."

In the context of sacrifices and the like, the term *dharma* (duty/virtue) is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) in the sense of being a generator [of merit]. The figurative meaning of the word *dharma* is that which is purposeful and is taught by the Veda. In the statement "One desiring to practice sorcery (*abhicāra*) should sacrifice with the Śyena," the word *śyena* is used figuratively for the Śyena-sacrifice. The word *abhicāra* has a figurative meaning in the sense of violence consisting of acts such as striking with weapons, which is conducive to the death of an enemy. The word *adharma* (unrighteousness/non-virtue) has a figurative meaning in the sense of that which is taught by the Veda to be a means to an undesirable result.

In the case of the suffix *ti* in the word "yajeta" (*one should sacrifice*), it is accepted that although there is identity in the delimiting factor (the verbal root), there is a distinct denoted meaning due to the difference in the objects [of the action], as this is a portion of the verbal expression (*ākhyāta*). The aspect of being an object (*viṣayatva*) which depends on the mind is the meaning of "intendedness" (*uddeśyatva*). The denotable meaning (*śakyārtha*) is the activity of the instigator of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*). That from which something is invariably understood is its denoted meaning (*vācya*). In other cases, however, the power (*śakti*) is a particular intention, and the denotable meaning is the intended object.

The Mīmāṃsakas hold that [the denotation of the verbal suffix] occurs either in the birth (jāti), the individual (vyakti), or the relation (sambandha); elsewhere, it is by means of indication (lakṣaṇā). In the case of the word *yajeta* ("one should sacrifice"), the understanding is: "one who possesses an activity conducive to an inclination favorable to the sacrifice. Either the *bhāvanā* itself is the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*), or the property of being an instigation (*pravartanātva*) is the delimitor of its primary meaning. Favorability (*anukūlatva*) is the state of being a generator (*janakatva*). The term *āpta* refers to a speaker of truth—whether in common worldly usage or in the Veda—who is an instructor of what is beneficial and harmful, distinct from one who causes deception; or else, it is the instruction itself that is indicated (*lakṣaṇā*).

In the Vedic context, the meaning expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers is the activity of instigation, dispatching, injunction, or efficient-force (*bhāvanā*). In worldly sentences, the meaning expressed by the optative suffix and others consists of commanding, ordering, requesting, permitting, assenting, directing, or inciting a person to act according to their own will; that is, it is the efficient-force (*bhāvanā*) consisting of the instigation of a person. This is a particularity of knowledge, a particularity of desire, or a particularity of intention residing in the person in the world. Whether in the case of a command in a worldly sentence or an activity in a Vedic one, "activity-ness" (*vyāpāratva*)—that is, "instigating-ness" (*pravartanātva*)—is the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*).

In the context of "operation" (*vyāpāra*), there is a power (*śakti*) whose form is subtle, residing in the instigation (*pravartanā*) termed "operation. The delimitors of this capacity (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) are the properties of being an optative suffix (*liṅ*), a subjunctive suffix (*leṭ*), an imperative suffix (*loṭ*), and so forth. Thus, the operation of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is the meaning of the optative suffixes and the like. In common worldly usage, however, by means of a non-abandoning metaphorical indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*), activity proceeds according to the nature of such an operation; furthermore, the status of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) is also the meaning of the optative suffixes and the like. Maṇḍana Miśra, on the other hand, maintains that the meaning of the optative suffixes and the like is the status of being an instigation (*pravartanātva*) which consists in being a means to a desired end.

Maṇḍanamiśra, however, maintains that the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is "being a motivator" (*pravartanātva*), which consists in being the means to achieve what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). Pārthasārathi, on the other hand, holds that the optative suffix and so forth denote a power residing in themselves called "denotation" (*abhidhā*), which is conducive to the expression of the objective productive energy (*arthabhāvanā*); this power, as a motivator, is the meaning of the optative suffix and so forth, and the cognition of this motivator is the cause of engagement.

Now, following the hearing of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, there occurs an inclination to act; thus, the knowledge of the optative suffix and the like is useful for the production of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), by way of generating that complex which consists of the desire to bring about the very nature of that [inclination]. And this knowledge consists of the knowledge that [the action] is not connected with a powerful undesirable consequence, the knowledge that it is achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*), and the knowledge that it is a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). This is [effected] through the knowledge of the optative suffix and the like.

The Naiyāyikas maintain that the suffix *liṅ* and others possess a triple denotation (*śakti*) consisting of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*), and not being followed by a more powerful undesired consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*), because these three together produce the cognition [of the action]. The Mīmāṃsakas, however, hold that the cognition of "not being followed by a more powerful undesired consequence" is an obstacle to activity; therefore, its mere absence—existing as a factual state (*svarūpasan*)—is the cause of activity. Consequently, the triad of being a means to a desired end and so forth is not the meaning of *liṅ* and other such suffixes. Rather, the objective productive energy (*arthabhāvanā*) is to be accomplished by the verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*), and their relationship is one of the means and the end to be accomplished.
The cognition of the suffix is the instrumental cause of knowledge, since the two productive energies exist eternally together.

Now, since an injunctive word possesses the capacity to denote an operation that causes the knowledge of the objective *bhāvanā*—which consists of the person's activity—it generates activity by means of [that] knowledge. And this operation has knowledge as its cause; it consists of the knowledge of itself, the knowledge of its capacity, and the knowledge of itself as qualified by that capacity. Among these, either of the first two constitutes the verbal *bhāvanā*, while the third serves as its instrument (*karaṇa*). For a person who possesses the knowledge of excellence (*prāśastya*) and an attachment (*rāga*) toward the result, there arises activity.

The nature of *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) consists in fulfilling the requirement for illumination regarding the instruments (*karaṇa*). A specific *arthavāda* is that which makes known a particular excellence (*prāśastya*). Excellence (*prāśastya*)—as defined in the context of injunctive *arthavādas*—is characterized as the production of a desired result greater than the suffering produced by the action, while being free from the accompaniment of a powerful undesirable consequence, and existing in a state of co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the delimitor of the status of being enjoined (*vidheyatāvacchedaka*).

In prohibitive arthavādas, however, "unfitness" (aprāśastya)—defined as being a means to greater suffering than the result of the action—is indicated by way of its co-occurrence with the delimiting property of that which is prohibited. In every sentence, there is indication (lakṣaṇā). When indication resides in a single word, the other words serve to indicate the intended meaning (tātparya). Śabdabhāvanā is a specific operation of the verbal suffix *liṅ* and so forth, which has the objective-efficient-force (*arthabhāvanā*)—characterized by the activity of a person—as its goal; it is denoted by the verbal suffix *liṅ* through its aspect as *liṅ*-ness.

Effort (*prayatna*) directed toward actions such as sacrifice, which is produced by the desire for results such as heaven and possesses an operation (*vyāpāra*), is called *arthabhāvanā*. Effort alone is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) in general. Alternatively, the meaning of the verbal suffix in general is an operation possessing the capacity to produce a result. This operation takes the form of activities beginning with the placing of fuel on the fire (*agnyanvādhāna*) and ending with the satiation of Brahmins; in the case of a chariot, it consists of the disjoining and conjoining of the front and rear parts; and in the case of an axe, it consists of the raising and lowering [of the blade].

Effort (*prayatna*) is obtainable from the verbal root alone. Even [mental states] such as knowledge and desire are operations (*vyāpāra*). Now, there is a distinct suitability (*anukūlya*) of the operation directed toward sacrifice with respect to heaven; there is a distinct suitability of the operation of cooking with respect to rice; there is a distinct suitability of the operation of drinking medicine with respect to health; and there is a distinct suitability of the operation of cooking with respect to rice. Thus, a specific operation characterized by a distinct suitability possesses a distinctness relative to the meaning of each respective verbal root. Therefore—

The meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*) in its generality is not *bhāvanā*. Rather, the meaning is the *artha-bhāvanā*—distinct from the meaning of the verbal root—which constitutes the general meaning of the suffix of the verb (*ākhyāta*). This consists of the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), namely the fruit (*phala*) such as heaven, which serves as a qualification for the person; the purpose (*artha*), namely the sacrifice and its subsidiaries such as the *prayāja* offerings; and also the various purposes that serve those purposes. The person who, desiring heaven and desiring the *apūrva*, engages in the performance of the sacrifice through both the *bhāvanā* expressed by the verbal suffix and the [verbal root] is the "eligible person" (*adhikārī*), which is used here in a figurative sense (*lākṣaṇika*).

Apūrva is fourfold or manifold: it is technical (pāribhāṣika) in its nature as the relationship between sacrifice and heaven; it is etymological (yaugika); or it is figurative (lākṣaṇika). For the sake of the fruit, there is the *phalāpūrva*; for that, the *samūhāpūrva*; for those, the *utpattyapūrvas*; and for those, the *aṅgāpūrvas*. From their commencement until the final state of being experienced, these various [apūrvas] are accumulated, commenced, and being performed; they possess diverse denotable meanings, or alternatively—

They are defined by a single commonality: as being an activity (*vyāpāra*), as being the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), and as being the unprecedented (*apūrva*). There is only one word expressive of the unprecedented that conveys the "great" unprecedented (*mahāpūrva*), namely the knowledge of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*); whereas the individual subordinate verbal suffixes convey their respective intermediate unprecedented effects.

Because there are innumerable verbal roots (*dhātu*) and because their respective individual manifestations are also numerous, those [verbal forms] produced as being attached to specific single roots denote *bhāvanā* (efficient force). Consequently, the *bhāvanās* of sacrifice (*yāga*), giving (*dāna*), and offering (*homa*) are mutually distinct. When there is a difference in *bhāvanā*, there is also a difference in its instrumental factors (*karaṇa*), due to the difference in the object denoted by another non-synonymous word. Thus, even when there is repeated performance, there is a difference in the acts such as sacrificing, and also a difference in the *apūrva* (transcendental result) obtainable from that verbal form. There is also a difference based on the relationship between the beneficiary and the benefactor.

By virtue of the connection with numbers such as duality and plurality, even through a single finite verb (*tiṅanta*) word, there arise multiple sacrifices and multiple productive energies (*bhāvanā*s) dependent on those numbers; thus it is in many ways. Due to the difference in the "form" (*rūpa*) characterized by the substance and the deity, there is a difference in the productive energy. A mass of milk that has become solidified is for the sake of the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture); the water remaining is for the sake of the substance *vājina* (whey). *Vāja* means food. Through differences in another word, repetition, number, name, quality, and a different context, actions are differentiated, and consequently, the productive energies are also differentiated.

Veda-hood (*vedatva*) consists in being a collection of impersonal statements that convey a purposeful meaning. The nature of an injunction (*vidhitva*) consists in being a portion of the Veda that makes known an unknown object and so forth; in this context, the word "soma" is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to mean that which contains soma. Mantra-hood (*mantratva*) consists in being a statement that causes one to remember an object connected with the ritual performance. In the case of "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," there is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *udbhid* in a qualified injunction, meaning "one should bring about cattle by means of a sacrifice characterized by the *udbhid*."

In the injunction "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *citrayā*," six diverse substances to be offered—curd, honey, milk, rice-gruel, water, and rice—are prescribed for the sacrifice. Because the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) consists of multiple substances, it is denoted by the word *citrayā*. Thus, the term *citrayā* refers to the *citrayā* sacrifice; in this context, the word *citrayā* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*). In the case of "He offers the *agnihotra*," since Agni is restated and Prajāpati is enjoined as a deity conjoined with him, the name is established through the principle of "a scripture describing that [deity]"; thus, the ritual named *agnihotra* is of the nature of a *homa* (libation).

In the injunction "One desiring to practice sorcery should sacrifice with the Śyena," the sacrifice named Śyena is praised by means of the praise of the hawk (Śyena) through the metaphorical application of the name; thus, the sacrifice named Śyena is the ritual action (*karman*).

In the case of "One should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva," since the Vaiśvadeva is a sacrifice consisting of a collection of eight [offerings] beginning with the Āgneya—as evidenced by the existence of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) in the form of a statement of established fact, "When the Viśvedevas sacrificed together, that became the Vaiśvadeva-nature of the Vaiśvadeva"—the Vaiśvadeva is established as the name of the ritual action (*karma-nāmadheya*) by virtue of that "scripture which proclaims what already exists" (*tat-prakhya-śāstra*).

A prohibitive injunction (*niṣedhavidhi*), while establishing a cessation (*nivartanā*), induces the person to refrain by implying that the prohibited act—such as the eating of *kalañja*—is a means to an undesirable end for others, thereby securing its own status as a cause of cessation. Furthermore, the inherent nature of the negative particle (*nañ*) is to convey a meaning that is contrary to the object denoted by the word with which it is syntactically associated. Thus, in the sentence "One should not eat *kalañja*," there is a cessation (*nivartanā*) which is contrary to the instigation (*pravartanā*) expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*), and this cessation opposes the instigation that would otherwise produce a person's inclination toward the act of eating having *kalañja* as its object.

The meaning of a sentence [containing] a negative particle (*nañ*) is that which excludes what is contradictory to the meaning of the word with which it is uttered in proximity. However, in the case of "One should not look at the rising sun," the negative particle has the sense of excluding the act of looking at the rising sun. Since this occurs within a section on injunctions (*vidhi-prakaraṇa*), the negation is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*)—a negation consistent with the injunction—employed to indicate that something other than the prohibited act must be performed. The word *vrata* (vow) is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of what ought to be done (*kartavyārtha*). In the view of exclusion (*paryudāsa-pakṣa*), the sense of what ought to be done is obtained; in the view of absolute negation (*niṣedha-pakṣa*), it is difficult to obtain.

The intention not to look, which is contrary to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), is indicated through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*). Thus, the meaning of the sentence is: "One should effect [the result] by means of the intention not to look at the sun. From the scriptural injunction, "In sacrifices, one performs the *yeyajāmahe*," there is the application of the *yeyajāmahe* chant. However, by the prohibition, "Not in the *anuyāja*s," there would be a prohibition that one should not perform the *yeyajāmahe* in the *anuyāja*s. In a case where a prohibition is preceded by a prior application (*prāptipūrvaka-pratiṣedha*), there would be an option (*vikalpa*), but not sublation (*bādha*), because the basis for the application of the prohibitive scripture [is found] in another scripture.

Because contradiction is untenable, and because if one were to assume both alternatives, there would arise the contingency of partial invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) regarding one side; therefore, one does not resort to a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), but rather resorts to an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). The understanding of the sentence-meaning is as follows: "One should perform the chanting of the *yeyajāmaha* mantra in sacrifices other than the *anuyāja*s. Here, the negative particle (*nañ*) has a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇikatva*) with respect to "other than the *anuyāja*s. By way of restating (*anuvāda*) the *yeyajāmaha* which is already established by a general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*), its applicability to the domain other than the *anuyāja*s is enjoined.

Exclusion (*paryudāsa*) has the sense of restricting [the application] to that which is other than the [prohibited] object; subsumption (*upasaṃhāra*) has the sense of further restricting it. It is a prohibition of what is prompted by natural inclination (*rāga*), but not of what is the subject of a scriptural injunction; thus, there is a prohibition of that which causes a deficiency in the sacrifice, as well as an injunction for the performance of its opposite. In cases of praise or censure, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*).

An *arthavāda* consists of praise (*praśaṃsā*), censure (*nindā*), traditional narratives by others (*parakṛti*), and accounts of ancient events (*purākalpa*). The statement "The face of one who knows thus shines" is for the purpose of praise. Expressions such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity" possess meaningfulness because they communicate the excellence of the matter to be enjoined.

The prohibition, "Silver must not be given on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*)," possesses purposefulness by making known the censure of giving silver—through the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating that "He wept; that is the origin of Rudra's name" and "the ancestors weep [if silver is given]"—which implies that gold should be given instead. When there is a contradiction with other means of valid knowledge, an explanatory passage is called a figurative statement (*guṇavāda*). In the case of "The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is the sun," the quality of being as radiant as the sun is conveyed here through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

An *arthavāda* that conveys a matter already known through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is an *anuvāda* (restatement), as in "Fire is the remedy for cold," because the fact that fire is opposed to cold is already perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). An *arthavāda* that conveys a matter not contradicted by other means of valid cognition and not previously established by them is a *bhūtārthavāda* (factual explanatory statement), as in "Indra raised his thunderbolt against Vṛtra. Now, regarding the originative injunction (*utpattividhi*): in the case of "One offers the *agnihotra*," the injunction that conveys merely the essential nature of the ritual act is "By means of the *agnihotra* oblation, one should effect the desired result."

In the view of Guru [Prabhākara], the word "injunction" (*vidhi*) refers to words such as the optative suffix (*liṅg*) and so forth, as well as their meaning. In the view of Bhartṛhari, its meaning is *bhāvanā*, which is a specific operation of the word; in the view of Guru, it is the *apūrva* (unprecedented force) known as *niyoga*. And that [apūrva] belongs to the qualified agent who possesses [the conditions for eligibility] such as being alive. In the case of the fire-oblation (*homa*) and so forth, the apūrva is to be accomplished by human effort (*kṛti*). Alternatively, the apūrva itself serves as the purpose, such as the destruction of sin. The sacrifice has two forms: the material substance and the deity. Regarding the sacrifice, there are two things to be understood: either the generic property of being a substance (*dravyatva*) or the generic property of being a deity (*devatātva*), while the two—the specific substance and the specific deity—are what are indicated (*lakṣya*).

The application-rule (*viniyoga-vidhi*) is that which makes known the relationship between the subordinate and the principal, such as "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*). The word *vājapeya* denotes the substance, namely the drinkable liquor (*peya-surā*). Sovereignty (*svārājya*) is the fruit and the principal, while the sacrifice (*yāga*) is subordinate; and within the sacrifice, the substance is subordinate.
