Subordination (*aṅgatva*), which consists in being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*), is also made known by the injunction. In some cases, subordination is made known by the injunction acting in conjunction with a direct statement (*śruti*)—whether as an enjoining agent, a denoting agent, or an applicatory agent—that is characterized by independence.

The status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) is indicated by hearing a word in the *liṅ*, *leṭ*, or *loṭ* [optative] moods; by hearing the word "vrīhīn" (rice grains); and by hearing a word that generates the cognition of a relationship. Furthermore, the status of being an auxiliary is known through syntactical application (*vibhakti-viniyoga*). The term "implication" (*ākṣepa*) is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) for inference (*anumāna*) and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). The agent, though not directly expressed by the word, is brought forth by the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) and becomes "verbal" (*śābda*) through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as is the case with the connection to number. The capacity residing in the word or in the meaning is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) based on conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).

A sentence (*vākya*) consists of the co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) of words in the relationship of principal and subordinate. "The *juhū* ladle is made by means of *parṇa*-wood; by the *juhū* alone is the transcendental result (*apūrva*) produced. A primary rite (*prakṛti*) is that which teaches all the constituent parts (*aṅga*), while a modified rite (*vikṛti*) is that which does not teach all the parts. Context (*prakaraṇa*) is the mutual requirement (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*) as to "what" and "how. Context related to the primary productive energy (*bhāvanā*) is the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*); context related to the productive energy of the subordinate parts is the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*).

*Sandaṃśa* (the "tongs") is the state of being enjoined between two subsidiary elements that are themselves enjoined by reference to a single [other] subsidiary element. *Sthāna* (position) is commonality of location; and that *sthāna* has two types as its objects: *krama* (sequence) and *samākhyā* (name). A *yaugika-śabda* (etymological word) is one possessing the power of its individual parts, such as *adhvaryavaḥ pācakāḥ* ("the Adhvaryus are the cooks"). A *samākhyā* (name) possessing the power of the whole is one like *adhvaryavaḥ pācakāḥ* [where the whole term denotes the group]. A *rūḍha* (conventional) word possessing the power of the whole is one such as "cow" (*go*) and so forth.

A *yogarūḍha* (etymological-conventional) term, such as *paṅkaja* ("lotus"), functions through a combination of the power of its constituent parts (*avayava-śakti*) and the power of the whole (*samudāya-śakti*). A *yaugikarūḍha* (etymological-conventional) term, such as *udbhid*, possesses both independent etymological power and independent conventional power. Acts such as threshing (*avaghāta*) and sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) are directly contributing auxiliaries (*sannipatyopakāraka*). Acts such as the *prayāja* offerings are indirectly contributing auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*). An *āśrayikarma* (substrate-act), which consists of the form of the material (*dravya*) and the deity (*devatā*), is a technical designation (*paribhāṣikī saṃjñā*). A rule that makes known the sequence is an injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*). Sequence (*krama*) is extension (*vitati*), [or] priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*).

*Śruti* is the direct statement of the Veda. *Arthakrama* (order by purpose) is the determination of sequence based on utility. *Pāṭhakrama* (order of recitation) is the sequence of sentences that convey the meaning of ritual acts. *Upasthitikrama* (order of proximity) and *Sthānakrama* (order of position). *Mukhyakrama* (order of the principal) is the sequence of subsidiaries dependent upon the order of the primary act. *Adhikāravidhi* (qualification injunction) is the rule that makes known the ownership of the fruit produced by the ritual act. For verbal roots expressing meaning, their inherent power (*śakti*) is the auxiliary factor. The *Ucchedanyāya* (the maxim of cutting): even when both [ends] are released together, there is still an expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

Even when there is a simultaneous interruption (*apaccheda*) regarding one or both [the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ], everything must be given again. A restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is an injunction that brings about the attainment of an alternative means which was not previously obtained, when there is a choice between various means and methods for accomplishing a single action. It is an injunction that brings about the attainment of what was not obtained as an option. An exclusive injunction (*parisaṃkhyāvidhi*) is an injunction intended to exclude the other when two options are simultaneously available. For example, in the statement "five five-nailed animals are to be eaten," the meaning of the sentence is the exclusion of eating non-five-nailed animals; this is an exclusive injunction based on secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*).

The *gārhapatya*, *dākṣiṇātya*, *āhavanīya*, *rābha*, *āvasathya*, *nāciketa*, *pāvaka*, *pavamāna*, and *śuci* are specific designations for the sacrificial fires (*agni*). The *vara* is that which indicates the gift of a cow. The *puroḍāśa* is a sacrificial oblation consisting of rice grains cooked in milk; it is also known by the name *caru*. The *sruva* is a sacrificial vessel for libations with a rounded tip, shaped like a ladle, and hollow in the middle. The *sruc* is a sacrificial vessel for libations with a curved beak-like tip, hollow in the middle. The *viṃśaty-āhuti* constitutes the *agnihotra*.

The rite called Agnihotra should be understood, by way of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā), as comprising its entire ritual complex, beginning from the installation of the sacred fires (agnyādhāna) and ending with the sprinkling of water—purified in the Agnihotra vessel—upon one's own head. In this regard, those desiring cattle, heaven, sensory power, a village, food, vigor, strength, or splendor are the qualified performers (adhikārin). Gruel (yavāgū) is that which is cooked until soft with rice grains, yet remains thin and watery. The fire of marriage is the domestic fire (gṛhyāgni), also known as the Gārhapatya.

The term *agnināśa* (loss of fire) is figurative (*lākṣaṇika*) when there is a decline in the duties pertaining to the sacred fires. The ritual action that begins on the morning of the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) and is completed during the forenoon of the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipat*) is what is denoted by the term *pūrṇamāsa*. The ritual action that begins on the morning of the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and is completed during the forenoon of the first day of the lunar fortnight is characterized by the term *darśa*. Taken together, the two sets of evening and morning oblations (*sāyaṃprātar-homa*) constitute the single ritual of *agnihotra*. At the *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, however, these are performed separately. The materials are either rice (*vrīhi*) or barley (*yava*).

The mantras known as *yājyās* and *puronuvākyās*, which are recited in both the Yajurveda and the Ṛgveda; the ritual sweeping of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), its consecration, smearing it with cow dung, drawing three lines each [on the ground], removing the loose soil, and so forth; first, a handful of *kuśa* grass—either in pairs or in odd numbers up to nine—which constitutes the *prastara*; the *camasa*, a square wooden vessel; the *yoktra*, a cord made of *muñja* grass for binding the waist of the sacrificer’s wife; and the heated water known as *madantī*.

A wooden vessel (*kāṣṭhapātra*) is a stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) for mixing flour with water. A *veda* is a specific handful of *darbha* grass. *Anvāhārya* refers to the cooked rice (*odana*) to be given as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). The pouring out of the oblation (*havirnirvāpa*) is the placing of the oblation, which is kept on a mat, into separate vessels by the handful. *Nyan-ci* means downward-facing vessels with their openings turned down. *Phalīkaraṇa* is the threshing of dehusked rice grains to make them bright and clean. A *dṛṣadupala* is a grinding stone used for pounding rice grains.

Having formed balls from flour and rice powder by kneading them with warm water, one should offer two well-cooked cakes (*puroḍāśa*) in the fire—one dedicated to Agni alone, and one dedicated to Agni and Soma together. The *dhātavaḥ* are blades of *darbha* grass used as sticks, turned three times. *Upastaraṇa* is the pouring of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) into the vessel with the *sruva* ladle. *Abhighāraṇa* is the sprinkling of clarified butter over the *puroḍāśa* with the *sruva*; this is to be performed for solid sacrificial substances. The *sāmidhenyaḥ* are the verses known by that name. *Āghāra* is the stream of clarified butter poured with the *sruva*.

There are also the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and streams of clarified butter (*ājyadhārā*). The five fore-offerings (*prayāja*) are: the fuel-stick (*samit*), Tanūnapāt, Iḍ, Barhis, and the utterance of *svāhā*. For four of these, those same deities are the recipients; for the fifth, the deities are Sviṣṭakṛt, the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), the fore-offerings, and the after-offerings (*anuyāja*). The *praiṣa* is the formula of direction. The *prāśitra* is the portion of the oblation being given to the Brahman priest for consumption. Sviṣṭakṛt is the name of a specific fire. The *anuyājahomas* consist of rice cooked with milk.

The *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings; the removal of the calves (*vatsāpākaraṇa*), which is the driving away of the calves from their mothers; and the act of curdling (*ātañcana*), which consists of pouring a small amount of curd into the boiled milk and placing that vessel on the sling.

The *sruva* ladle is made of *khadira* wood, with a circular cavity the size of a thumb-joint hollowed out at the front half; it is one *aratni* in length, including the handle, and is the instrument for offering oblations. The *sphya* is made of *khadira* wood, shaped like a sword, one *aratni* in length, and includes a handle; it is a specific type of wooden spoon. The *juhū* ladle is made of *palāśa* wood; its handle is solid and without a hollow, it possesses a single spout resembling the beak of a swan, its bowl (*puṣkara*) is half a span in width and hollowed to that same depth, and it is a vessel for offering oblations. Furthermore, there is the *parṇamayī juhū*.

The *upabhṛt* is a sacrificial vessel made of *palāśa* wood, with its base and handle intact, provided with a single spout resembling a swan’s beak, having a bowl half a span in size and a cavity of the same measure. The *dhruvā* is a sacrificial vessel made of *vikaṅkata* wood, with its base and handle intact, provided with a single spout resembling a swan’s beak, having a bowl half a span in size and a cavity of the same measure.

The *agnihotra-havanī* (offering ladle for the Agnihotra) has its bottom pierced with a hole, is provided with a single spout resembling the beak of a swan, has a bowl (*puṣkara*) measuring one span (*prādeśa*) in width, and is dug out to that same depth; it is made of *vikaṅkata* wood and serves as a sacrificial vessel. The *agnihotra-sruva* (small offering spoon for the Agnihotra) is like a *sruva*, provided with a single spout resembling the beak of a swan, made of *vikaṅkata* wood, and serves as a sacrificial vessel. The *ulūkhala* (mortar) is a vessel for threshing, characterized by its purpose, and is made of *varaṇa* wood.

The *musala* (pestle) is characterized by its purpose; it is made of *varaṇa* wood and serves as an instrument for threshing. The *kūrca* is a broom, arm-length in size, shaped like a seat, and made of grass. The *iḍāpātrī* is one cubit long, with a handle four fingers wide, held in the middle, and having a circumference of four fingers. The *puroḍāśapātrī* is one span long, square in shape, and has a circular cavity six fingers deep.

The *upaveṣa*—the means for the ritual preparation—is one cubit (*śamyā*) in length, shaped like a mace (*gadā*), with a broad and sharp tip resembling the bud of a lotus. The *prāśitraharaṇa*—the means for removing the sacrificial porridge (*caru*)—is shaped like a cow’s ear. The winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) is made of bamboo, with a circumference appropriate to its purpose.

The *camasa* is a vessel made of *varaṇa* wood, with a handle three finger-breadths long, four finger-breadths high, and six finger-breadths wide; it is one span in length and serves as the implement for bringing forward the water. The *yoktra* is a cord made of *mūñja* grass used for binding the waist of the wife. The *madantī* vessel is a bronze bowl used for mixing and for heating the water. The *mekṣaṇa* is an implement made of *varaṇa* wood, one cubit (*aratni*) in length, used for mixing the flour.

The *anvāhāryasthālī* is a cooking vessel made of copper or bell-metal, sufficient for cooking enough food for four persons. The *piṣṭalepapātra* is a vessel made from the *varaṇa* tree. The *phalīkaraṇapātra* is a vessel one span (*prādeśa*) long, also made from the *varaṇa* tree. The *śakaṭa* is a cart-shaped cart. The *kapālāni* are nineteen fragments of broken vessels, such as square pieces and so forth. The *idhmakāṣṭhāni* are fuel-sticks.

Kuśas: Darbha grass used as implements for spreading on the altar, making purifiers (pavitra), and surrounding the sacrificial ground. Seating mats made of darbha grass and wooden seats. Yavāgū: rice gruel intended for the Agnihotra sacrifice. Kumbhī: an earthen vessel for boiling milk. Abhidhātrī: a rope for tethering the cow. Nidāne: at the time of milking, a rope for binding the [cow's] feet and a rope for binding the calf. Vṛkṣakhaṇḍakīlaka: a wooden post, octagonal in shape, for tethering the calf. Rope for binding the calf.

The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is a wedge-shaped block of wood with eight corners; the first chip cut from it is the *svaru*, used for sprinkling the animal. The *caṣāla* is a knob placed on the top of the post so that the tip of the post is not visible, serving as a means of identification. The *hṛdayaśūla* is a thorny spike. *Pṛṣadājya* is clarified butter mixed with curds. *Upākaraṇa* is the formal dedication of the animal to the deity, preceded by touching it. *Tanūnapāt* or *Narāśaṃsa* is Agni.

The *vapā* (omentum) is white-reddish, soft, very thin, and internal skin. The *yakṛt* is a piece of liver-meat. The *vṛkyau* are two glandular masses located near the ribs. The *savyaṃ bāhumūlam* is the left armpit. The *iḍā* is the cooked omentum in the form of a sacrificial cake (*purāḍāśa*). The *svadhiti* is a small knife. The *medas* is fat, appearing like worn-out cloth, which envelops the heart and takes the form of the omentum. The oily essence contained in the cooking vessel is the *vasā*. There are eleven deities at the *anuyāja* and other rites, and they are named: Barhis, Dvāra, Uṣāsānaktā, Joṣṭrī, Ūrjā, Āhuti, Hotṛ, and Narāśaṃsa.

The three deities of this [offering] are Vanaspati, Barhis, and Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. The *caṣāla* is the heart-spike (*hṛdayaśūla*) or thorn. The *abhri* is for the purpose of digging the pit for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). There are four seasonal festivals (*parvan*): the Vaiśvadeva, the Varuṇapraghāsas, the Sākamedhas, and the Śunāsīrīya. These sacrifices are designated by the term "festival" (*parvan*) on the full moon days.

*Avabhṛtha* is the final purificatory bath at the conclusion of a sacrifice. *Śunāsīra* refers to Śuna (Indra) and Sīra (Vāyu); the festival dedicated to them is the *Śunāsīrīya* parvan. The mantras beginning with "Whatever offense against the gods... (*yad devā devaheḍanam*) and the oblations performed with them are called *Kūśmāṇḍas*. *Soma* is a specific creeper—"the *śyāmā*, *amlā*, *niṣparṇā*, *kṣīriṇī*, and *tvaci-māṃsalā*; it is phlegmatic, emetic, a climbing vine known as *soma*, and the food of goats. A sacrifice in which that *soma* substance is used is the basis for the application of the term *soma*.

In the *somayāga*, there are twelve *stotras* (hymns of praise), the last of which is called the *agniṣṭoma*; therefore, the sacrifice itself is also named *agniṣṭoma*. The names [of other sacrifices] are derived from the *stotras*: *ukthya*, *atirātra*, and so forth. Even the *pūtika* creeper serves as a substitute for the *soma* plant. For the purpose of selecting the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the *vastu-prabhṛti* is sent up to the *samprāvāka*. The group of *adhvaryu* priests consists of: *adhvaryu*, *pratiprasthātṛ*, *neṣṭṛ*, and *unnetṛ*. The group of *brahmā* priests consists of: *brahmā*, *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*, *āgnīdhra*, and *potṛ*.

The *hotṛ* group consists of: the *hotṛ*, the *maitrāvaruṇa*, the *acchāvāka*, and the *grāvastut*. The *udgātṛ* group consists of: the *udgātṛ*, the *prastotṛ*, the *pratihartṛ*, and the *subrahmaṇya*. The *sadasya* is the seventeenth officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). The hall, covered with beams (*vaṃśa*) extending eastward for the purpose of roofing and supporting, is called by the names *prācīnavaṃśā* or *vimitā*. A net made of reeds (*iṣīkā*) is used for binding the hair on the wife’s head. *Pathyā Svasti* is the deity.

*Vicayana* is the removal and purification of grass and other fibers from the midst of the *soma*. *Pravargya* is the name of the ritual. Among the materials for the *pravargya*, there is the earthen vessel called the *mahāvīra*, which is filled with clarified butter and milk mixed with substances such as earth from other worlds, has an internal cavity, and possesses three openings. The *āsandī* is a seat made of *muñja* grass. The *dhṛṣṭī* are two wooden sticks used for removing embers. The *methī* is a post for tethering cows. The *śaṅku* is a peg or stake. The *rukma* is a circular object made of deer skin.

The rope for binding the feet; the *viśākhadāma*, the rope for binding the calf; the pouring of milk into heated metal; the name associated with these [ritual acts]; *vamrayaḥ*—termites, white ants, and white ants; the *pravargya* rite, which consists of the rejoining of the head of Viṣṇu, whose head was severed by the snapping of the bowstring, taking the form of the rejoining of the head of Jña; the *mahāvīra* vessel, which is the form of the head of the sacrifice; the *upasat*, a preliminary *iṣṭi* sacrifice; *subrahmaṇyā*—Indra; the *ṛtvij* who performs that ritual act is the *subrahmaṇya*.

The Gārhapatya fire is located behind; that which is known as the Prājahita is [the fire] in front. The water from a pond used for increasing the pressed Soma juice is designated as *vasatīvarī*. A *śastra* is a recitation; a *stotra* is a hymn of praise. *Karambha* is barley flour mixed with clarified butter (*ājya*). *Parivāpa* is parched grain (*lāja*). *Payasyā* is curdled milk (*āmikṣā*). A *graha* is a vessel. The *aṃśu-graha* vessel and the *adābhya-graha* vessel are one and the same. The *upāṃśu-graha* is [a cup not drawn from a stream]; the *adhārā-graha* are those cups to be drawn from a stream (*dhārā*). *Somāṃśavaḥ* are the tufts of crushed Soma stalks.

The *ṛṣīja* is a portion of grass from which the essence has been taken and which is sapless. The *antaryāma-graha* is the vessel for the internal draught. The *bahiṣpavamāna* is the chant; it consists of the *ṛc*s used as *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses during the chant. The *ṛtugrahas* are the vessels for the draughts dedicated to the seasonal deities, such as Spring and the others. The *mārjālīya* is the shed for the purpose of cleansing. The *khara* is the shed for depositing the vessels. There are twelve *ṛtugrahas*, which are the vessels named after the months. The *pratigara* is the chant being recited in response. The *nārāśaṃsa-homa* is the offering of drops of the substance from the *camasa* cups shaken over the fire; these are the *nārāśaṃsa-camasas*.

*Praudhaśastra*: a hymn bearing that name. *Cātvāla*: a sacrificial pit suitable for placing the antelope horn. *Marutvatīya*: a hymn dedicated to the Maruts. *Anavastrāvita*: boiled rice (*odana*) from which the water has not been drained. *Dadhidrapsa*: a small portion of curd. *Rājāsandī*: the throne-seat upon which the Soma juice is placed prior to the sacrifice.

The *ṣoḍaśa-stotra* is so called because it consists of sixteen hymns; the cup associated with it is the *ṣoḍaśī-graha*, and the seasonal sacrifice (*ṛtu*) is also termed *ṣoḍaśī*. At the end of the stream-cups (*dhārā-graha*), one should draw the *ṣoḍaśī* cup—a stream-cup—into a four-cornered vessel. For the *āśvina-graha* and its stotra, the Aśvinī-kumāras are the deities. The sacrifices named Agniṣṭoma, Atyagniṣṭoma, Vājapeya, and Aptoryāma are the specific forms of the Soma-sacrifice (*saṃsthā*). The Vājapeya is characterized by twenty-one initiations (*dīkṣā*), stotras, and sacrificial porridges (*caru*); it is further distinguished as the Āpta-vājapeya and the Kuru-vājapeya.

There are seventeen *prayāja* offerings here. The sacrifice by which Prajāpati obtained cattle is the *aptoryāma* sacrifice; it has twenty-nine *stotra*s. The specific sacrifices are to be understood from the *Śrautasūtras* and other such texts. In the third pressing (*savana*) during the night-round (*rātriparyāya*), there is the *rātriśastra* hymn. There are twenty-nine *stotra*s here. The numbers of the *stotra*s are the *stomas*. A *stoma* is a specific type of repetition within a *stotra*, denoted by the term *stoma*. *Triṇava* is twenty-seven; *trivṛt* is the number nine.

The word *kuśa* is technical (*lākṣaṇika*) or conventional (*rūḍha*) for a specific kind of light wood from the *udumbara* tree, one span long, with a sharp point, and planed on one side. *Citi* refers to the altars (*sthaṇḍila*), which are distinct in shape like those of the hawk and other birds. *Ukhā* is an earthen vessel; having placed the vessel over the fire in the *ukhā*, one should perform the four *viṣṇukrama* strides, and so forth—this is the *viṣṇukramaṇa*. There are eight oblations of the *devasū* offerings.

The animal sacrifice known as *sautrāmaṇī* consists of the *carakasautrāmaṇī* and the *kaukilasautrāmaṇī*. The *rājasūya* is a composite form consisting of many *iṣṭi*s, two animal sacrifices (*paśuyāga*s), seven *darvihoma*s, and six *somayāga*s. One should have the King drink the juice extracted from crushed *vaṭa* sprouts. That milk which turns into curd without the addition of a coagulant is called "solidified" (*mūrta*).

In that [sacrifice], one should throw jujube fruits (*badara*) which have been churned by oneself; having cooked a sacrificial pap (*caru*) with that and broken rice grains, one should worship Mitra with it. One who holds the title of *kṣattr* (a warrior-noble) should cause the story of Śunaḥśepa to be recited. Now, the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) is for the sovereign (*samrāj*), the universal emperor (*sārvabhauma*). For an ordinary king, there is the royal sacrifice (*rājayajña*). The "horse-sacrifice" involves the employment of great equipment. In the horse-sacrifice, there is the *sāṃgrahiṇī* offering. In the human-sacrifice (*puruṣamedha*), there are human victims; living persons themselves are to be offered and relinquished.

In the *puruṣamedha* (human sacrifice), Śunaḥśepa was released while still alive; likewise, in the *sarvamedha*, the human victim is released immediately after the ritual immolation (*upākaraṇa*). The *sava*s are Soma sacrifices to be completed in a single day (*ekāha*), twelve in number, each dedicated to a specific deity. The *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* are the designations for the opening and concluding days, respectively, which are understood through Vedic textual procedures and related rites. In the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice, there are the *tryanīkā* arrangements of the cups (*graha*). The *gavāmayana* is a sacrificial session (*satra*) lasting a year, performed by the cows.
The verbal roots (dhātus) have speech as their primary form; words are considered to be produced from them.
The suffixes (pratyayas) are attached to them, and from those [suffixes] the case-factors (kārakas) arise. 483.

The "root-elements" (*mūladhātu*) are those such as *pañca* (five) and *bhū* (earth), which are recited in the grammatical lists (*gaṇa*). The "sutra-elements" (*sautradhātu*) are those such as *skambhū* and *jup*, which are mentioned only in the sūtras. The "derivative elements" (*yaugikadhātu*) are those ending in suffixes, such as *pāci* (one who cooks) and *pipakṣa* (one who desires to cook), which convey meanings obtainable from their own constituent parts. Words such as *titikṣā* (endurance) are indeed derivative, as they include within themselves the nature of the root meaning along with its suffix. Furthermore, even common worldly words such as *hindola* (swing) and *āndola* (to swing) are considered verbal roots.

Verbal roots such as *gam* (to go) and *bhū* (to be) are capable of producing the cognition of agency—whether primary or secondary—for the sake of their own meaning, namely the acts of going, arising, or proceeding, which constitute the sense of the *parasmaipada*. This is because from forms such as *saṃgacchate* and *bhavate*, one understands the agency of reaching (*saṅgati*) or coming into being (*prāpti*), respectively; thus, they are *ātmanepadin* (self-reflexive) with respect to such meanings. Roots like *yaj* (to sacrifice) and *kṛ* (to do), however, are both *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* (ubhayapadī) with respect to the act of sacrificing and so forth, because from forms such as *yajati* and *karoti* as well as *yajate* and *kurute*, one likewise understands the agency of performing the sacrifice and other such acts.

Verbal roots with a vowel as their *anubandha* (indicatory letter) belong to the *bhū*, *ad*, *div*, etc., classes; those with *ñ* as their *anubandha* include *kṛñ*, *suñ*, and others; and those with *ṇ* as their *anubandha* include *bhāvī* and so forth. These [roots] stand in syntactic expectancy (*sākāṅkṣa*) with two words expressing the agenthood [of the action]. However, roots ending in the desiderative suffix *san* take the word of their own base form [as the agent]. Although the roots *smṛ* and *dṛś* are *parasmaipada* (active voice), they take the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) when ending in *san*.

Verbs ending in *yaṅ* such as *haṃs*, those ending in *yaṅ* such as *bobhū*, those with the marker *ṅ* such as *śīṅ*, and the *rucādi* group require the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) alone when expressing the agent. However, those that differ from both [the aforementioned] and the middle voice require the active voice (*parasmaipada*) alone.

A suffix (*pratyaya*) is divided into five types: case-endings (*vibhakti*), verbal roots (*dhātu*), nominal suffixes (*taddhita*), primary suffixes (*kṛt*), and suffixes such as *kap*. A suffix that possesses a power delimited by the intermediate genus "number-ness" (*saṃkhyātva*) is a case-ending (*vibhakti*); it is of two kinds based on the distinction between *sup* (nominal endings) and *tiṅ* (verbal endings). That word which is capable of producing a cognition of the connection of its own base-meaning as the predicate with respect to its own referent as the subject is a case-ending, such as *sup* and so forth.

In the case of "ghaṭam" (the pot), the objecthood (*karmatva*) belongs to the pot; in "pacati" (he cooks) and similar cases, it is the effort (*kṛti*) belonging to the cooking. Thus, by way of the relationship between the subject and the predicate, the suffix generates a cognition in which its own meaning is the predicate relative to the meaning of the stem (*prakṛtyartha*). In "nīlo ghaṭaḥ" (the blue pot), there is a "pot non-different from blue" (*nīlābhinna-ghaṭaḥ*). Therein, identity (*tādātmya*) belongs to the blue. Once the understanding of the intermediate sentence-meaning—namely, that "identity belongs to the blue"—has occurred, the resulting cognition is: "the pot possesses identity with blueness. The case-endings (*sup*) are those which generate a cognition of the number of their own meaning as being related to the meaning of the stem as its qualificand (*dharmika*).

The nominative case (*prathamā*) is that which is not inherently capable of conveying a cognition of the base-meaning as having a property distinct from identity with itself. When this [nominative] follows a qualifying word (*viśeṣaṇapada*), it conveys the connection of the base-meaning with identity (*tādātmya*) as its own expressed referent. The dual of the nominative is delimited by the phoneme *au*, and the plural is delimited by the phoneme *jas*. The same applies to other cases and numbers.

In the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*), there is an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) because the status of being an *niyojya* (the person to be directed), which is presented first and is distinct from identity, is construed with the sacrifice; for the Mīmāṃsakas accept that the status of being an *niyojya*—namely, being understood as "this is my duty"—and the cognition thereof apply to the sacrifice and other ritual acts.

Since the state of being the locus (*ādheyatva*) is accepted as being related—by way of a relation such as "being produced by an effort" (*kṛtisādhyatva*), which is part of the meaning of the injunction—to the effort (*kṛti*) and so forth, there is non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in both those cases; therefore, another definition is given: the nominative case (*sup*) is that which is the cause for the cognition of the connection of the meaning of a *tiṅ*-suffix with something delimited by the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*). In the example *yajeta* ("one should sacrifice"), the property of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) and so forth, which is the meaning of the *tiṅ*-suffix, is connected only in its own form, and not as delimited by the meaning of the verbal root, namely, the sacrifice (*yāga*) and so forth.

The nature of the second case-ending (*dvitīyā-vibhakti*) is the state of being similar to a *sup*-suffix that is conducive to the experience of the objecthood (*karmatva*) of an action such as cooking, which is established by a verbal root such as *pac* (to cook). Although [suffixes] like *am* in "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*) do not cause the experience of objecthood with respect to actions such as cooking, they are still included because they are of the same class as those suffixes that do cause the experience of objecthood. The nature of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā-vibhakti*) is the state of being similar to a *sup*-suffix that is conducive to the cognition of the connection of instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) with respect to the meaning of a root such as *pac*. For example: "It is cooked by Rāma" (*rāmeṇa pacyate*).

The nature of the fourth case (*caturthītva*) consists in being a type of *sup*-suffix that possesses the capacity to convey a recipient (*sampradāna*) characterized by the act of giving (*dadāti*). Example: *rāmāya dadāti* ("He gives to Rāma"). The nature of the fifth case (*pañcamītva*) consists in being a type of *sup*-suffix that is conducive to conveying a separation (*vibhāga*) whose locus is qualified by a property delimited by the sense-restrictor (*tāvacchedaka*) of the root *pat*. Example: *vṛkṣātparṇaṃ patati* ("A leaf falls from the tree"). The nature of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhītva*) consists in being a *sup*-suffix other than the first case (*prathamā*), while not being inherently incapable of conveying a relation of its own meaning (*svārtha*) as residing in the meaning of the verbal base (*dhātu*) ending in *ti*. Example: *rāmasya śaraḥ* ("Rāma's arrow").

The status of being a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) consists in being of the same class as a *sup*-suffix that causes the cognition of its own meaning as having an object that is the agent of an act of harming, or as having the nature of an act of harming; for example, in *mṛgasya hiṃsakaḥ* ("the killer of a deer"). Alternatively, the genitive is a *sup*-suffix capable of denoting either a general relation or the state of being an existent (*satvatva*); for example, in *rājñaḥ prajā* ("the subjects of the king") and *nṛpasya kośaḥ* ("the treasury of the king"). The status of being a locative (*saptamī*) consists in being of the same class as a *sup*-suffix that is conducive to the cognition of its own meaning as the locus (*ādheyatva*) residing in an object delimited by a form that serves as the delimitor of the meaning of the verbal root *pac* ("to cook"); for example, in *śākasūpayoḥ pācakaḥ* ("the cooker of vegetables and soup").

The locative case (*saptamī*) is that *sup*-suffix which is attached to the sense of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatā*) or being contained therein (*ādheyatva*), as in "odor in the earth" (*pṛthivyāṃ gandhaḥ*) or "Caitra in [the presence of] Bali" (*balini caitre*). In these cases, there is the odor’s quality of being a property of the earth, and Caitra’s status as the locus of the object. The definition of the locative is: being a *sup*-suffix with the same phonetic sequence (*samānānupūrvīka*) as another *sup*-suffix that conveys the relation of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) in connection with the meaning of the nominal stem. Thus, from "in Caitra" (*caitre*), the cognition is: "the locus-ness belonging to Caitra. A grammatical factor (*kāraka*) is a meaning of a *sup*-suffix that serves as a qualifier (*prakāra*) within the meaning of the verbal root. A case-ending (*vibhakti*) is a *sup*-suffix that makes known a factor through its own function (*vṛtti*), while making known something other than the factor itself. A factor (*kāraka*) is an entity that has become a qualifier of the action (*kriyā*).

The "residual" (śeṣa) relation is that which is other than a *kāraka*, i.e., remaining after the *kārakas* have been accounted for; it is not a *kāraka*. A meaning expressed by a nominal suffix (*subartha*) is a *kāraka* with respect to a particular action expressed by a verbal root (*dhātu*) if it appears as the mode of connection (*prakāra*) in the relation with that action.

In examples such as "He goes to the village," "He sees the jar," "He cuts with an axe," "He cognizes [it] as a jar," "He is cooked by Caitra," "It exists as a jar," "He gives to the Brahmin," "He is angry with the son," "He falls from the tree," "He fears the tiger," "He cooks in the pot," and "It shines in the mother-of-pearl," the objectness (*karmatva*) and other relations presented by the second case (*dvitīyā*) and subsequent cases appear as qualifiers (*prakārībhūta*) within the meanings of the verbal roots—such as going and so forth. That objectness and so forth is the meaning of the nominal suffix (*sub-artha*).

In the present context, the *kāraka* (grammatical participant) is that which possesses the status of being an object (*karman*) and so forth with respect to a particular action established by a particular verbal root (*dhātu*). That very meaning of a nominal stem (*nāmartha*), delimited by the meaning of a nominal suffix (*subartha*), is designated as a non-*kāraka* with respect to the meaning of such a verbal root. The relation expressed by the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*) does not appear as a qualifier (*prakārībhūya*) within the meaning of the verbal root; therefore, the relation is not a *kāraka*, the genitive expressing it is not a *kāraka*-expressing suffix, and it is not a *kāraka*-case ending (*kārakavibhakti*).

In the expression "he gives the cloth to the washerman" (*rajakasya vastraṃ dadāti*), the genitive case on "cloth" (*vastram*) conveys a relationship characterized by being the object to be processed (*pariṣkāryatva*). In cases such as "the cooker of rice" (*taṇḍulasya pācakaḥ*) or "what is to be eaten by Maitra" (*maitrasya bhoktavyam*), the genitive denotes a *kāraka*—specifically the objective (*karman*) or the agent (*kartṛ*)—because it is prescribed that the genitive expresses the agent or the object when used with a verbal noun (*kṛdanta*) whose meaning is based on the root-meaning, such as "cooking. [As stated: "A physician should provide treatment for teachers, Brahmins, ascetics, and the destitute."

"In *svabheṣajaiḥ padmasyānukaroty eṣa kumārīmukhamaṇḍalaḥ* (this orb of the maiden’s face imitates the lotus by means of its own remedies), *sā lakṣmīr upakurute yathā pareṣām* (she, Lakṣmī, benefits others as much as possible), *mātuḥ smarati* (he remembers his mother), *caurasya hinasti* (he harms the thief), *jalasyopakurute* (he benefits the water)," and so forth—in these cases, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) expresses the sense of a *kāraka* when joined with a specific action. In the rule "provided there is possession of a common property" (*sāmānyavattve sati*), the locative case (*saptamī*) is used after *sati*; this has the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), meaning that there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between [the word ending in] *sati* and the following word.

In the expressions "it occurs to me," "it flashes before me," and "it pleases me," since the self (asmadādi) appears as the locus (*ādheyatā*) of the cognition, desire, and intention denoted by *pratibhā*, there would be the contingency of the locative case (*saptamī*); however, by virtue of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used instead, and not because [the relation] is delimited by the general category of relation (*sambandhatva*). Alternatively, the word "in the mind" (*citte*) should be supplied as an ellipsis; thus, the locative case functions as a kāraka. 483.

Verbal cognition is the cognition of a relation (*anvaya-bodha*); the relation is a connection between meanings that are mutually expectant (*ākāṅkṣita*). Meanings are grasped through a word’s function (*vṛtti*) and are related to one another by virtue of semantic competency (*yogyatā*). (Verse 484) Verbal cognition has a relation as its object, and these relations are manifested by the mutual expectancy of semantically competent word-meanings. Now, in the case of the perception of a jar, there exists a subject-object relation (*viṣayatā*) residing in the conjunction and other relations between the jar and its properties such as "jar-ness" or color, which is brought about by the qualifier-relation (*viśeṣaṇatā*). In the case of inference, the subject-object relation residing in the fire is brought about by the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*), while the subject-object relation residing in the conjunction of the fire with the mountain is brought about by the knowledge of the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

In the case of the comparison [in "The gavaya is like a cow"], the objectivity residing in the gavaya is brought about by visual contact (*cakṣuḥ-saṃsarga*), while the objectivity residing in the relation of denoter and denoted (*vācya-vācakabhāva*) is brought about by the cognition of similarity (*sādṛśya-jñāna*). Regarding the question: what brings about the objectivity of ownership (*svatva*), non-difference (*abheda*), and so forth in the case of "the king’s man" (*rājapuruṣa*), and how does the cognition of relations such as ownership and non-difference occur in verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*)?—the answer is: the relation between the two word-meanings is a relation of ownership where the king is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and the man is the substratum (*anuyogin*), [arising] through the force of syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).

It shines forth; thus it is everywhere. A relation such as identity (*abheda*) possesses an objectivity (*viṣayatā*) that is brought about by expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). In the case of "blue pot" (*nīlaghaṭa*), the objectivity residing in the word is brought about by auditory perception (*śrāvaṇapratyakṣa*); the objectivity of the meaning is brought about by the word (*pada*); and the objectivity of the relation of identity and so forth is brought about by the cognition of expectancy. In the case of the expanded form "the pot is blue" (*nīlo ghaṭaḥ*), the meaning of the adjective's case-ending is the qualifier (*prakāra*)—namely, identity—and not a relation; the resulting cognition is "the pot is possessed of identity with the blue."

In the view that the case-ending of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇavibhakti*) is devoid of meaning, however, the relation of non-difference (*abheda*) and so forth is what is manifested by the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). The case-ending of the qualifier serves the purpose of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*); the resulting cognition is, for example, "the jar is qualified by blue through the relation of non-difference," or "the person is qualified by the king through the relation of ownership. In verbal cognition, the relation between two word-meanings is twofold: non-difference and difference. Non-difference is a single relation; even if there are many instances, they are one insofar as they possess the nature of non-difference.

As for these distinctions, they are distinct from their own essential nature (*svarūpa*), yet they are themselves the very things being distinguished. In the case of "the floor possesses a jar" (*ghaṭavad bhūtalam*), there is the relation of the contained and the container (*ādheyādhārabhāva*). In "there is no jar on the floor" (*bhūtale ghaṭo nāsti*), there is the relation of the counter-correlate and the substratum (*pratiyogyanuyogibhāva*). In cases such as "knowledge of a jar" (*ghaṭe jñānam*) or "desire for liberation" (*mokṣe icchā*), there is the relation of the object and the subject (*viṣayaviṣayibhāva*), meaning knowledge having the jar as its object and desire having liberation as its object. Each of these—distinction, containment, substratum-ness, and so forth—is itself distinct.

Relations of identity appear through the requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*) for the meaning presented by a word standing immediately before it and sharing the same case-ending as the meaning of a single nominal stem; however, identity does not appear between the meanings of two words that possess conflicting case-endings.

"Having the same case-ending" (*svasamānavibhaktikatva*) means having a case-ending that is of the same class as the case-ending of its own base (*svaprakṛtika*). This "sameness of class" (*sājātya*) is determined by the property of being *prathamā* (nominative) and so forth, which are the classifiers of case-endings. In the expression "a hundred Brāhmaṇas" (*śataṃ brāhmaṇāḥ*), the authoritative cognition—namely, "Brāhmaṇas non-different from a hundred"—is indeed authoritative, because of the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) stating, "The words beginning with *viṃśati* (twenty) are always used in the singular. However, in this case, there is no "sameness of sequence" (*samānānupūrvokatva*) between the suffixes *su* and *jas*; furthermore, there is no "sameness of number" (*samānavacanakatva*), nor is there "sameness of gender" (*samānaliṅgakatva*).

In this way, there is no identity of gender (samānaliṅgakatva) in the expression "perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition" or "the ancestors are the deities. How, then, can such usage be authoritative? It is as follows: where the number intended by the case-ending following the word expressing the qualifier is not incompatible with the number [intended] for the qualified object, there is a rule that the words expressing the qualifier and the qualified must agree in number.

And thus, in the aforementioned instances, because there is no lack of desire to express the number one—which is contrary to the plurality that is the intended meaning of the case-ending following the word *veda*—and because there is no rule requiring grammatical agreement (samānavacanakatva), the use of non-agreement is authoritative (*pramāṇa*). Since "the means of valid cognition" (*pramitikaraṇa*) is the definition of *pramāṇa*, the property of being a means of valid cognition (*pramitikaraṇatva*), which is the delimitor of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthatāvacchedaka*), is intended to be one and the same across all four Vedas; therefore, the number one is construed with the "means of valid cognition."

However, this is not the case with the Vedas; for the status of being a means of verbal cognition (śābdapramākaraṇatva) is a single property residing in all words, delimited by the universal "word-ness" (śabdatva), and thus there is no lack of fitness. Now, according to the rule that "in the absence of a sublation, a word-meaning connects with a word-meaning, but not with a mere part [of it]," the connection of oneness with the single constituent part consisting of the instrument of cognition is faultless—just as in the expression "the rice is prepared," where oneness connects with the generic class "rice-ness" due to the sublation of its connection with multiple individual rice grains. Thus, there is no defect here.

Alternatively, in the Vedas, the number one (ekatva) is construed with [the sacrifice] through the relation of "possessing the delimitor of the meaning of the prakṛti (verbal root) whose locus is itself"; it is not, however, multiple unities. Furthermore, the meaning of the word [denoting number] is precisely "being devoid of a second similar entity," where "similarity" consists in being a unity that does not delimit the counter-correlativity of a difference residing in something belonging to its own class; it is not mere unity alone. This is because, in the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), such a unity residing in the animal is intended, since the transcendental result (*apūrva*) is established in the sacrifice performed by means of that [animal].

And co-occurrence (*sājātya*) consists in the possession of the delimitor of the primary meaning (*prakṛtyarthatāvacchedaka*) as qualified by being related to the referent of the word uttered in its own proximity. In the case of "There is a jar here" (*atra ghaṭo'sti*), there is no lack of established precedent (*aprasiddhi*), because it conveys a unity that is not a delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the difference residing in the jar existing in this location.

In a state where many pots exist, the usage [of the singular] occurs because of the oneness of the genus (*jāti*). In the expression "the three together are the cause," the word "cause" (*hetu*) refers to the collection (*samudāya*) as delimited by the collection-nature (*samudāyatva*), which is the delimitor of the causal efficiency (*prayojakatāvacchedaka*). Thus, there is the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of oneness with the collection-nature. The resulting cognition is: "The three possess that property which is the collection-nature, characterized by oneness, and which is the delimitor of the causal efficiency for the production of the effect."

In poetry, a triad constitutes the cause; however, with respect to fire, grass, flint, and gems possess causality even when they are not combined. Now, regarding the aphorism "The meaning of a word consists of genus, configuration, and individual," it is intended that the status of being the "meaning of a word"—which takes the form of the word's power residing in these three—is conceived as a single unity; that is, the state of being denotable by a word is pervasively present across the triad of genus, configuration, and individual.

The "objectness" (padārthatva) in an object consists in the word's power (padaśakti) being related to it by the relation of "determining factor-ness" (nirūpakatva); thus, the state of being an object is the state of being determined by the word's power. In the statement, "Perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition," the singular number residing in the instrumentality of valid cognition is sublated with respect to the four [means], and therefore the plural form "pramāṇāni" is used. In the phrase, "The ancestors are the deities," the singularity residing in the deityhood is not intended to be expressed, whereas the plurality in the qualifier is intended.

"Having that as its base" (*svaprakṛtikatva*) means being recalled as immediately following itself; "self" (*sva*) refers to that which is its base. By this, even in the case of "the curd is beautiful" (*dadhi sundaram*), where there is no case-ending following the word "curd" (*dadhi*), there is no deficiency regarding agreement in number and so forth, because it is accepted that in a compound (*vyāsa*), there is a recollection of the elided case-ending.

The state of having a case-ending (vibhakti) similar to that of such [a word] also consists in being cognized as occurring immediately prior to a case-ending of that kind; by this, there is no impairment to the cognition of syntactic relation (anvaya-bodha) in the case of "idaṃ dadhi" even when a case-ending does not follow the qualifying word.

Now, regarding the verbal cognition "the pot is non-blue" (*anīlo ghaṭaḥ*)—wherein the meaning is "a pot non-different from the non-blue"—the cause is the knowledge of *ākāṅkṣā* (syntactic expectancy). This *ākāṅkṣā* consists in either: (1) the state of the word "non-blue" (*nīla*), which is a nominative-ending term, being co-occurrent with the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*), which is the nominative-ending subject; or (2) the state of the word "non-blue" occurring immediately before the word "pot," or the state of the word "pot" occurring immediately after the word "non-blue. Where this [expectancy] is absent, as in the case of "the pot of the non-blue" (*nīlasya ghaṭaḥ*), there is no cognition of identity (*abheda*). However, in the case of "bring the blue pot" (*nīlaṃ ghaṭam ānaya*), [such expectancy exists].

The state of having "blue" as its subsequent object (nīlottara-karmatva) has no syntactic connection (anvaya) anywhere, because the case-ending of the qualifier serves only for grammatical correctness (sādhutvārtha). In non-compound (asamāsa) instances, that [case-ending] has non-difference (abheda) as its meaning; however, in a compound, non-difference is understood through the relational capacity (saṃsargamaryādā), since the case-ending is elided.

Now, non-difference (*abheda*) is the absence of difference (*bhedābhāva*). When difference is absent, there is a "fragmented power" (*khaṇḍaśakti*) due to the case-ending (*vibhakti*) being a qualifier; however, the apprehension of the qualified (*viśiṣṭalābha*) occurs by virtue of syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). In the expression "a blue pot" (*nīlo ghaṭaḥ*), the word-meaning "blue" is construed with the meaning of the case-ending as "difference" (*bheda*) by way of being its counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*); that "difference" is construed with "absence" (*abhāva*) by way of being its counter-correlative; and that "absence" is construed with the "pot" as the substantive (*viśeṣyatva*). Thus, the resulting cognition is: "The pot is the substantive of the absence of the difference from blue. In the expressions "wealthy by means of grain" (*dhānyena dhanavān*) and "a Gārgya by lineage" (*gotreṇa gārgyaḥ*), [the same principle applies].

In cases involving secondary nominal suffixes (*upapada-vibhakti*), the absence of conflicting case-endings is not the cause for the cognition of non-difference as a qualifier; therefore, there arises the cognition: "one who possesses wealth non-different from grain" (*dhānyābhinna-dhanavān*) or "Gārgya non-different from the lineage" (*gotrābhinna-gārgyaḥ*). This is because the Vārttika rule, *prakṛtyādibhya upasaṃkhyānam* ("an addition regarding words such as *prakṛti*"), prescribes the third (instrumental) case-ending in the sense of non-difference.

In such cases as "charming by nature," "generally a performer of sacrifices," "he goes on level ground," "he goes on uneven ground," "he buys grain for two *droṇas*," "he takes cattle for five [coins]," or "he travels with ease or with difficulty," the use of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is correct. Now, in the case of "the pot is non-measurable" (*aprameyo ghaṭaḥ*), there is no established instance of a difference from that which is measurable (*prameya-bheda*). Furthermore, in the case of "the pot possesses a neck and so forth" (*kambugrīvādimān ghaṭaḥ*), there is no established instance of a difference qualified by a heavy (complex) property (*guru-dharma-avacchinna-bheda*).

To this, it is said: the absence of difference delimited by the respective individuality (*tattadvyaktitva*) of those various individuals appears as their relation; its status as a relation consists in its being an absence whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is the difference from those respective individuals, or alternatively, an absence whose counter-correlate is the difference from those respective individuals. In the case of "The blue (cloth) is a jar," there exists in the jar only that difference whose counter-correlate is delimited by the respective individuality of the blue object consisting of the cloth. In the case of "The jar is cognizable" (*prameya*),...

The existence [of the property] of having a counter-correlativity delimited by the specific individuality (vyaktitva) of each appearing entity is well-established. In the case of "the pot possesses a conch-shaped neck and so forth," the connection with the difference [between the pot and others] is well-known through the relation of having a counter-correlativity delimited by the specific individuality of the appearing entity possessing a conch-shaped neck and so forth.

Now, non-difference (*abheda*) has identity (*tādātmya*) as its meaning. And that [identity] is a property (*dharma*) residing in only one [of the two relata]; and this residence (*vṛtti*) appears through the relation of connection (*saṃsargamaryādayā*). Furthermore, the property consists of such things as the specific individuality (*tattadvyaktitva*) [of that object], which is easily grasped through the cognitive proximity of universals (*sāmānyapratyāsatti*). Non-difference appears through the relation of connection; even there, the recurring non-difference is the relation.

Identity (*tādātmya*) is a unique property residing in itself (*svavṛttyasādhāraṇadharma*). Uniqueness (*asādhāraṇya*) consists in residing in one thing alone. And that [uniqueness] is properly defined as being other than that which is qualified by difference (*bheda*), through the two relations of co-inherence with itself (*svasāmānādhikaraṇya*) and residing in its own counter-correlative (*svapratiyogivṛttitva*). It is not, however, of the nature of a collection (*kūṭa*) of absences of differences delimited by each respective individuality (*tattadvyaktitva*). For if it were so, then in the cases "The pot is not blue" and "Blue is not blue," validity would result by taking an absence of the non-existence of the difference from a single instance of blue.

In a context where, in the absence of the negative particle (*nañ*), the possession of a certain property by a certain subject is understood through a certain relation and in a certain form, it is established by grammatical convention (*vyutpatti*) that in such a context the negative particle conveys the absence of that property—characterized by that same relation and that same property—as residing in that same subject; therefore, the negative particle does not convey difference (*bheda*).

In the case of "taking a non-blue pot" (*anīlaṃ ghaṭam ādāya*), however, there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the negative particle (*nañ*) as denoting that which possesses difference; this is because the word *anīla* refers to what is different from blue, in order to conform with its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *ghaṭa*. But when non-difference (*abheda*) is the qualifier (*prakāra*), as in "the pot is not blue" (*ghaṭo na nīlaḥ*), the absence of the absence of the difference from blue—which is the very nature of the difference from blue—is understood by the negative particle as having the property of being a difference (*bhedatva*). In the case of the expanded construction (*vyāsa*) "the pot is blue" (*nīlo ghaṭaḥ*), however, one must assume that the case-ending of the qualifier functions with respect to the relation (*saṃsarga*).

In the expressions "stokaṃ pacati" (he cooks slightly) and "mṛdu pacati" (he cooks gently), because of the requirement for semantic connection (*ākāṅkṣā*), there is a relation of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*); thus, the cognition is: "the agent possesses an act of cooking non-different from slightness" and "the agent possesses an act of cooking non-different from gentleness. This is because of the grammatical rule that adverbs are neuter and function as objects (*karmatva*). In the expression "stokaḥ pākaḥ" (a slight cooking), the suffix *ghañ* serves merely to indicate grammatical correctness; since it lacks a meaningful referent [as an object], the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) does not occur in "stokam. However, in the expression "stokaṃ sthīyate" (it is stayed slightly), the accusative case does occur because the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) has a meaningful referent, namely the present tense.

Where the intention (*tātparya*) pertains solely to the verbal root (*dhātu*), such as in the case of "cooking" (*pāka*), there is coreferentiality (*samānavibhaktitā*); thus, we have the expression *stokaḥ pākaḥ*. In cases where the number is conveyed by the case-ending following a word denoting that [verbal root], a causal complex for verbal cognition (*śābdabodhasāmagrī*) is required that possesses a cognitive object (*viṣayatā*) distinct from the qualifier-ness (*prakāratā*) delimited by the relation of identity (*abheda*). This occurs in instances such as *eko ghaṭaḥ* ("one pot") and *dvau ghaṭau* ("two pots"). However, in cases such as *nīlau ghaṭau* ("two blue pots"), duality is conveyed by the case-ending following the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*), and not by the case-ending following the word "blue" (*nīla*).

The singular number following a word that functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) is used solely for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*). Non-difference (*abheda*) is the relation of co-referentiality (*anvaya*) between two items presented in different forms; therefore, in cases such as "the pot is a pot," "staff-bearer is staff-bearer," or "he cooks the cooking," there is no cognition through a relation of non-difference. In the case of "the substance is a pot," there arises a cognition where the pot is the qualifier (*prakāra*) related by non-difference to the property of substantiality (*dravyatva*), by way of the relation of being the delimiting factor of the locus (*dharmitāvacchedakatā-sambandha*).

With respect to verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) inhering in the self (*ātman*), the cause is the presentation (*upasthiti*) and so forth, by way of inherence (*samavāya*). Verbal cognition occurs in the jar (*ghaṭa*) through the relation of subjecthood (*dharmitā*) as the objective content; in "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), it occurs through the relation of subject-determiningness (*dharmitāvacchedakatā*) as the objective content; [in the case of the quality white] in the white substance, it occurs through the relation of qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) as the objective content; and in "white-ness" (*śuklatva*), [it occurs through the same].

[In the case of] the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatā*) in the form of the delimitation of the mode (*prakāratāvacchedakatā*), [the cause is] by way of the relation of objecthood called "non-difference" (*abheda-saṃsarga*). However, in the case of the relation of non-difference, [the cause is] by way of the relation of objecthood called "non-difference. With respect to verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), the cause is the presentation (*upasthiti*) and so forth by way of relations such as objecthood. Because the presentation of word-meanings through the proximity of identical modes (*samānaprakāratā-pratyāsatti*) is the cause of verbal cognition, [the cause is] the presentation of word-meanings by way of relations such as objecthood.

By whatever relation a causal complex—delimited by a certain property (*yaddharmāvacchinna*) and producing an effect with respect to an effect delimited by another property (*taddharmāvacchinna*)—is required for the production of that effect delimited by the latter property, through that same relation. For instance, in the absence of the mental presentation (*padārthopasthiti*) of the referent generated by the word "substance" (*dravya*) with respect to substanceness (*dravyatva*) and so on via the relation of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*), there is no production of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) even with respect to the delimitation of the locus (*dharmitāvacchedakatā*) in the case of substanceness and so forth.

Even by one who possesses the verbal cognition delimited by that property, there is no production of a verbal cognition [of that same object]. With respect to a verbal cognition delimited by a particular property (D), the cause is the presentation of the word-meaning, which has that property (D) as its qualifier and is produced by a knowledge of the linguistic function (*vṛtti*) having that property (D) as its qualificandum.

Thus, with respect to that [cognition], the difference from that property (*taddharmabheda*) is the cause, by way of the relation of being the delimitation of the qualificandumness (*viśeṣyatāvacchedakatā*) as determined by the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) delimited by non-difference and delimited by that property. For the sake of understanding "That is a jar" (*sa ghaṭaḥ*), both the delimitation of the qualifierhood and the delimitation of the qualificandumness must be taken as non-delimited (*niravacchinna*). In "A jar is a jar" (*ghaṭo ghaṭaḥ*), there is no such understanding because of the absence of a difference between properties. In "A jar is a blue jar" (*ghaṭo nīlaghaṭaḥ*), there is understanding due to the difference between properties. [In the case of] "Substance is a jar" (*dravyaṃ ghaṭaḥ*... In this case, there is a cognition based on the difference between *dravyatva* (substanceness) and *ghaṭatva* (potness). With respect to a verbal cognition delimited by the property of being a verbal cognition (*śābdabuddhitva*), the cause is the difference between those two properties (*taddharmabheda*), related through the relation of being the delimitor of the objective reference (*viśeṣyatāvacchedakatā*)—which is itself determined by a mode (*prakāratā*) delimited by the relation of non-difference residing in those properties (*taddharmavṛttyabhedasambandhāvacchinnaprakāratānirūpita*). This [cause] is related [to the effect] through the relation of being the delimitor of the substratum of the locus of the complete distribution (*paryāptyanuyogitāvacchedakatva*).

And the subsistence of that property in the modehood [is established] by way of the relation of being the delimitor of the locus of the relative complement (paryāptyanuyogitāvacchedakatva), where the relative complement has as its counter-correlative (pratiyogitā) that which is delimited by the property of "being a deliminator" (avacchedakatātva) as determined by itself; here, "self" (sva) refers to the modehood delimited by the relation of identity (abheda).

Since the words *saḥ* (he) and *saḥ* (he) possess a denotative power (*śakti*) directed toward the possessor of a genus (*jātimat*), there is a modehood (*prakāratā*) and a qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) delimited by genus-ness (*jātitva*). In that context, to prevent the cognition "the possessor of a genus, the possessor of a genus" (*jātimān jātimān*), the difference between those properties (*taddharmabheda*) is also a separate cause for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), mediated by the relation of being the delimitation of the delimitation of the property-hood (*dharmitāvacchedakatāvacchedakatva*) which is itself the delimitation of the modehood delimited by that property (*taddharmāvacchinnāvacchedakatākaprakāratānirūpita*). In the case of "the possessor of a staff, the possessor of a staff" (*daṇḍavān daṇḍavān*), the same applies; there too, the difference between staff-ness (*daṇḍatva*) and so forth is a separate [cause].

Regarding causality: in cases such as "the possessor of a staff is the possessor of a staff" or "the possessor of a staff is the possessor of a genus," for the sake of understanding a relation of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*), one must stipulate that both types of delimiters (*avacchedakatā*) are "undelimited" (*niravacchinna*). However, in reality, the cause for a cognition with respect to a particular property (*taddharma*) is the difference from that property (*taddharma-bheda*), by way of the relation of being a content residing in something other than that property. In the case of "the pot is a pot," the causal complex for a difference in properties does not exist, and thus there is no cognition [of difference]. Likewise, in "the possessor of a pot is the possessor of a pot," there is no cognition [of difference]. And in "one" or "two," there is an absence of the cognition of a relation of difference.

In the case of "karma gacchati" (the object goes), there is no [such] cognition because of the identity between the property-delimiting factor (*dharmitāvacchedaka*)—which is "objecthood" (*karmatvatva*)—and the delimiting factor of the mode (*prakāratāvacchedakatāvacchedaka*), which is also "objecthood. Similarly, in "ghaṭo na ghaṭaḥ" (a pot is not a pot), there is no cognition because of the identity of "potness" (*ghaṭatva*). Thus ends the discussion on the verbal cognition of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya-śābdabodha*). || 484 ||

Now, the manner in which verbal cognition arises from difference and relation: the relations of difference include the owner-owned relationship (*svasvāmibhāva*), the counter-positive-substratum relationship (*pratiyogyanuyogibhāva*), the locus-located relationship (*ādhārādheyabhāva*), the state of being defined (*nirūpitatva*), the state of being conducive (*anukūlatva*), the state of having itself as the object (*svakarmakatva*), the state of having Caitra as the agent (*caitrakartṛkatva*), and so forth.

Verse 485: When a relation of difference is conveyed by a case-ending (*vibhakti*) or by a particle (*nipāta*), it serves as the cause for that cognition of difference; and in other instances, the cognition of difference occurs accordingly.

The understanding of a relation through difference (*bhedasambandha*) arises between the meaning of a nominal stem (*pratipadikārtha*) and the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*), as well as with the meaning of an affix (*pratyayārtha*) and the meaning of a particle (*nipātārtha*). With respect to a verbal cognition (*śābdabuddhi*) characterized by the property of being a verbal cognition, where the relation is the "subjectness" (*viśeṣyatā*) determined by a "qualifierhood" (*prakāratā*) residing in the meaning of a name, which is delimited by a relation of difference (*bhedasaṃsargāvacchinna*), [the following relations hold]: the relation between a king and a man—whether expressed by a case-ending (*vibhakti*) or a particle (*nipāta*) other than these—is the relation of owner and owned; that is, the relation of ownership (*svatva*) in the man belonging to the king.

With respect to a verbal cognition whose qualificandumhood is delimited by puruṣatva (person-ness) and whose qualifierhood is delimited by rājatva (kingship) as qualified by the relation of difference, the cause is the presentation of that meaning generated by the genitive case-ending (*ṅas*). In the sentence "The pot is not a cloth," the relation of difference between the pot and the cloth is characterized by the status of counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) and locus (*anuyogin*).

In the case of "the jar," the relation is the state of being qualified by a difference whose counter-correlate is the cloth. For the verbal cognition (śābdabodha) which has as its qualificandum (viśeṣyatā) delimited by "jar-ness" and which is determined by a mode (prakāratā) delimited by "difference-ness" and having a counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) delimited by "cloth-ness" as qualified by a relation delimited by difference, the cause is the mental presentation (upasthiti) of that object produced by the word *nañ* (the negative particle).

In the expression "he cooks rice" (*taṇḍulaṃ pacati*), there is the cognition that the objecthood (*karmatā*)—which consists of the substratum (*ādheyatā*)—resides in the rice, which is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), by means of a relation of difference consisting of being a substratum (*ādheyatā-sambandha*). In the expression "the face is like the moon" (*candra iva mukham*), the meaning of the nominal stem "moon" is construed with the meaning of the particle "like" (*iva*), namely similarity (*sādṛśya*), by means of a relation of difference consisting of being characterized (*nirūpitatva-sambandha*).

The similarity (*sādṛśya*) is construed with the face (*mukha*) by way of the relation of substratum; the cognition is: "the face possesses a similarity as defined by the moon. In the sentence "he cooks rice" (*taṇḍulaṃ pacati*), the cooking, which is the meaning of the verbal root, is construed with the effort (*kṛti*), which is the meaning of the verbal suffix, by way of the relation of being conducive (*anukūlatā*); [the result is] "an effort conducive to cooking. And that effort is construed with the agent (*kartṛ*) by way of the relation of substratum; [the result is] "one who possesses an effort conducive to cooking. In the sentence "one should not eat *kalañja*," regarding the eating which is the meaning of the verbal root, that which constitutes the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*)—

The meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is the absence of being a means to a desired end qualified by the lack of connection with a powerful undesirable result (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva-viśiṣṭeṣṭasādhanatva*). This [absence] is construed with the object of the action through the relation of *anuyogitā* (the state of being the locus of negation). Thus, the cognition is: "Eating *kalañja* possesses the absence of being a means to a desired end qualified by the lack of connection with a powerful undesirable result. In the view of the Guru Mīmāṃsaka, one should produce a *paṇḍāpūrva* characterized by the absence of eating *kalañja*. A *paṇḍāpūrva* is a fruitless *apūrva*; an *apūrva* is the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), which is of the nature of merit (*puṇya*).
